VOL. 56.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION.

Containing His Majesty's Declaration, That it is expedient that the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, on the Part of Great Britain; and commanding the said Lords and Commons to give their Attendance accordingly.

GEORGE R.
---
Whereas by the Fourth Article of the Articles of the Union of Great Britain and Ireland, as the same are ratified and confirmed by Two Acts of Parliament, the one passed in the Parliament of Great Britain, intituled, "An Act for the Union of Great Britain and Ireland," the other passed in the Parliament of Ireland,

also intituled, "An Act for the Union of Great Britain and Irelandto have Force and Effect from the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, it is provided, that if We, on or before the said First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, on which Day the Union is to take place as aforesaid, should declare, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, that it is expedient that the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland', on the Part of Great Britain; then the said Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should accordingly be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the said United Kingdom, on the Part of Great Britain: And whereas it is Our Intention to appoint Thursday the Twenty-second Day of January next ensuing for the assembling of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, by Proclamation under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom; We do judge it to be expedient that the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom, on the Part of Great Britain: And We do, pursuant to the said Articles of Union, and to the Acts of Parliament ratifying and confirming the fame, hereby declare, under Our Great Seal of Great Britain, that it is expedient that the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, on the Part of Great Britain j and the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain are accordingly to be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, on the Part of Great Britain; and the said Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, are hereby required and commanded to take Notice hereof, and to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, on the said Twenty-second Day of January next ensuing.

Given at Our Court at Saint James's, the Fifth Day of November One thousand Eight hundred, in the ' Forty-first Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION,

declaring His Majesty's Pleasure for holding the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and appointing the Time and Place of Meeting thereof.

GEORGE R.

WHereas, in pursuance of the Fourth Article of the Articles of Union between Great Britain and Ireland, as the same have been ratified and confirmed by Two Acts of Parliament, the one passed in the Parliament of Great Britain, and the other in the Parliament of Ireland, and both intituled, "An Act for the Union " of Great Britain and Ireland We have thought fit to

declare, by Our Royal Proclamation iliiied under Our Great Seal of Great Britain on. the Fifth Day of November last, that it was expedient that the Lords and Commons of the then Parliament of should be

Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, on the Part of Great Britain: And We did by the same Proclamation notify Our Intention to appoint Thursday the Twenty-second Day of January Instant for thealfembling of such First Parliament of the said United Kingdom, by Proclamation under the Great Seal of Our said United Kingdom: And whereas, by force and in pursuance of an Act passed in the Parliament of Ireland, and recited in and made Part of the said Two Act s for the Union of Great Britain and Ireland, and intituled, "An Act to regulate the Mode by which the Lords " Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons, to lerve in the Parliament of the United Kingdom on the Part of " Ireland shall be summoned and returned to the said " Parliament and in consequence of Our having by Our said Proclamation under Our Great Seal of Great Britain,of the Fifth Day of November last, declared that it was expedient that the Lords and Commons of the then Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom on the Part of Great Britain, Four Lords Spiritual, and Twenty-eight Lords Temporal, and One Hundred Commoners, have been appointed, cholen, and declared (according to the Circumstances of the several Cafes) to be the Members of the respective Houses of the said First Parliament of the said United Kingdom on the Part of Ireland: We do, by this Our Royal Proclamation under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with the Advice of Our Privy Council, declare and publish Our Will and Pleasure to be, and do hereby appoint, that Our First Parliament of the said United Kingdom shall meet and be holden at Our City of Westminster, on the said Twenty-second Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One; whereof the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs of Our said First Parliament of the said United Kingdom, and all others whom it may concern, are hereby to take Notice. And We do hereby direct and command, in pursuance of the said Fourth Article of the said Articles of Union, that the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, who are to serve in the said Parliament on the Part of Ireland, be returned in such Manner as by the said Act passed in the Parliament of Ireland to regulate the Mode by which the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons* to serve in the Parliament of the United Kingdom on the Part of Ireland, shall be summoned and returned to the said Parliament, such Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, are directed to be returned according to the Circumstances of each particular same of the several Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, so appointed, cholen, and declared to be the Members of the

- 3

ivspective Houses of the said United Kingdom on the Part of Ireland. And We do hereby further (with the Advice aforesaid) declare our Royal Will and Pleasure, that Our said Parliament of Our laid United Kingdom shall, on the said Twenty-second Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, be holden and fit for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs; and the said Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the said Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the said Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, are hereby required and commanded to give their Attendance accordingly at Westminster, on the said Twenty*second Day of January Instant.

Given at Our Court at Saint James's, the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, in the Forty-first Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION,

Declaring His Majesty's Pleasure concerning the Royal Stile and Titles appertaining to the Imperial Crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and its Dependencies, and also the Ensigns Armorial, Flags, and Banners thereof.

GEORGE R.

WHereas by the First Article of the Articles of Union of Great Britain and Ireland, ratified and confirmed by Two Acts of Parliament, the one passed in the Parliament of Great Britain, and the other in the Parliament of Ireland, and respectively intituled, "An Act for the Union of Great Britain and ," it was

declared. That the said Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland should upon this Day, being the First Day of January in the Year of Our Lord One thousand Eight hundred and One, for ever after 6e united into One Kingdom, by the Name of The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland; and that the Royal Stile and Titles appertaining to the Imperial Crown of the said United Kingdom and its Dependencies, and also the Ensigns Armorial, Flags, and Banners thereof, should be such as We, by Our Royal Proclamation, under the Great Seal of the said United Kingdom, should appoint; We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to appoint and declare that Our Royal Stile and Titles shall henceforth be accepted, taken, and used, as the same are set forth in Manner and Form following > that is to say, the same shall be express'ed in the Latin Tongue by these Words: — " GEORGIUS TERT1US, Dei Gratia, Britanniarum Rex, Fidei " DefenforAnd in the Tongue by these

Words: — " GEORGE the THIRD, by the Grace of " God, of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and <( Ireland King, Defender of the Faith." And that the Arms or Ensigns Armorial of the said United Kingdom shall be Quarterly, First and Fourth, England; Second,-Scotland; Third, Ireland: And it is Our Will and Pleasure, that there shall be borne therewith, on an Efco-cheon of Pretence, the Arms of Our Dominions in Germany, enfigned with the Eleftoral Bonnet. And it is Qur Will and Pleasure, that the Standard of the said United Kingdom shall be the same Quarterings as are hereinbefore declared to be the Arms or Ensigns Armorial of the said United Kingdom, with the El'cocheon of Pretence thereon hereinbefore described: And that the

Union Flag shall be Azure, the CrofTessSaltires of Saint Andrew and Saint Patrick quarterly per Saltire Counter changed Argent and Gules j the latter fimbriated of the Second; lurmounted by the Cross of Saint George of the Third, fimbriated as the Saltire. And Our Will and Pleasure further is, that the Stile and Titles aforesaid, and also the Arms or Ensigns Armorial aforesaid, shall be used henceforth, as far as conveniently may be, on all Occasions wherein Our Royal Stile and Titles, and Arms of Ensigns Armorial ought to be used. But nevertheless it is Our Will and Pleasure, that all such Gold, Silver, and Copper Monies as, on the Day before this First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, were current and lawful Monies of Great Britain, and all such Gold, Silver, and Copper Monies ds shall, on or after this Day, be coined by Our Authority with the like Impreffions, until Our Will and Pleasure shall be otherwise declared, shall be deemed and taken to be current and lawful Monies of the said United Kingdom in Great Britain , and that all such Gold, Silver, and Copper Monies as, on the Day before this First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, were current and lawful Monies of Ireland, and all such Gold and Silver, and Copper Monies as shall, on or after this Day, be coined by Our Authority with the like Impressions, until Our Will and Pleasure shall be otherwise declared, shall be deemed and taken to be current and lawful Monies of the said United Kingdom in Ireland; and all such Monies as shall have been coined for and issued in any of the Dominions of the said United Kingdom, and declared by Our Proclamation to be current and lawful Money of such Dominions respectively, bearing Our Stile, or Titles, or Arms, or Ensigns Armorial, or any Part or Parts thereof, and all Monies which shall hereafter be coined and issued according to such Proclamations, shall continue to be lawful and current Money of such Dominions respectively, notwithstanding such Change in Our Stile, Titles, and Arms, or Armorial Bearings respectively as aforesaid, until Our Pleasure shall be further declared thereupon. And all and every such Monies as aforesaid shall be received and taken in Payment in Great Britain and Ireland respectively, and in the Dominions thereunto belonging, after the Date of this Our Proclamation, in such Manner, and as of the like Value and Denomination as the same were received and taken before the Date hereof. And it is also Our Will and Pleasure that the several Dies and Marks, which have been used to denote the Stamp Duties, and all other Stamps and Marks and Inltruments, which, before the issuing of this Our Proclamation, shall have been in actual Ule for any Public Purpose, and in which Our Royal Stile and Titles, or Our Arms or Ensigns Armorial, or any Parts or Part thereof respectively, may be expressed, shall not, by reason of this Our Proclamation, or any Thing therein contained, be changed or altered, until the same may be conveniently so changed or altered, or until Our Pleasure shall be further declared thereupon: But that all such Dies, Stamps, Marks, and Instruments respectively, bearing Our Royal Stile and Titles, or Arms or Ensigns Armorial, used before this First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, or any Parts or Part of such Stile, Titles, or of such Arms or Ensigns Armorial, shall have the like Force and Effect, as the same had before the said First Day of January Instant.

Given at Our Court at Saint James's, the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, in the Forty-first Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

And the House being returned;

The Right honourable Thomas Pelham, one of the Knights of the Shire for the County of addressing

himtelf to the Deputy to the Clerk of the House (who Handing up, pointed to him, and then lat down) proposed to the House for their Speaker the Right honourable Henry Addington; in which Motion he was seconded by Charles Yorke, Esquire, one of the Knights of the Shire for the County of Cambridge.

The House then calling Mr. Addington to the Chair, he Hood up in his Place, and expressed the Sente he had of the Honour proposed to be conferred upon him, and submitted himself to the House.

And William Wilberforce, Esquire, one of the Knights of the Shire for the County of having spoken in

support of the Motion;

The House again unanimously called Mr. Addington to the Chair, and he was taken out of his Place by the said Mr. Pelham and Mr. Yorke, and conducted by them to the Chair; where. Handing on the upper Step, he returned his humble Acknowledgments to the House for the great Honour they had been pleated to confer upon him, by unanimously chooling him to be their Speaker.

And thereupon he fat down in the Chair; and then the Mace (which before lay under the Table) was laid upon the Table.

Then the Right honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson, commonly called Lord Hazukesbury, one of the Barons of the Town and Port of Rye, having congratulated Mr. Speaker ele<ft, moved that the House would adjourn till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

And the House accordingly adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

ble Petition to His Majesty, laid claim to all the ancient Rights and Privileges of the Commons, particularly that their Persons, their Estates, and Servants, might be free from Arrests, and all Molestations; that they may enjoy Liberty of Speech in all their Debates; may have Access to His Majesty's Royal Person whenever Occasion shall require; and that all their Proceedings may receive from His Majesty the most favourable Construction; which, he laid. His Majesty, by His said Commissioners, had confirmed to them, in as full and ample Manner as they have been at any Time granted or allowed by His Majesty, or any of His Royal Predecessors.

And then Mr. Speaker repeated his most respectful Acknowledgments to the House, for the Horfour they had done him.

Mr. Speaker then put the House in mind, that the first Thing to be done, was to take the Oaths of Allegiance and Supremacy, and make and subscribe the Declaration, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Abjuration, as by Law required.

And thereupon Mr. Speaker first alone, (landing upon the upper Step of the Chair, took the said first-mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration.

And, after him, several other Members took the said first-mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration; and one of the said Members having been returned to serve in the last Parliament of Great Britain, and not having taken his Seat there, delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and took and subscribed the Oath of Qualification, as by Law required.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had this Day attended His Majesty in the Hdufe of Peers; where His Majesty was pleased to make a most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

At a Crisis so important to the Interests of My People, I derive great Satisfaction from being enabled, for the first Time, to avail Myself of the Advice and Assistance of the Parliament of My United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

This memorable /Era, distinguished by the Accomplishment of a Measure calculated to augment and con-folidate the Strength and Resources of the Empire, and to cement more closely the Interests and Affections of My Subjects, will, I trust, be equally marked by that Vigour, Energy, and Firninels, which the Circumstances of our present Situation peculiarly require.

The unfortunate Course of Events on the Continent, and the Consequeuces which must be expected to relult from it, cannot fail to be Matter of Anxiety and Concern to all who have a just Feeling for the Security and Independence of Europe.

Your Astonishment, as well as your Regret, must be excited by the Conduct of those Powers whole Attention, at such a Period, appears to be more engaged in Endeavours to weaken the Naval Force of the Empire, which has hitherto oppoled so powerful an Obstacle to the inordinate Ambition of France, than in concerting the Means of mutual Defence against their common and increasing Danger.

The lleprefcntations which I directed to be made to the Court of VeterJl 'urgh,in Consequence of the Out-

rages committed against the Ships, Property, and Per-Ions, of My Subjects, have been treated with the utmost DilVelpect; and the Proceedings of which I complained have been aggravated by subsequent Acts of Injustice and Violence.

Under these Circumstances a Convention has been concluded by that Court with those of Copenhagen and Stockholm, the Object of which, as avowed by one of the contracting Parties, is to renew their'former Engagements for establishing by Force, a new Code of Maritime Law, inconliftent with the Rights and hostile to the Interests of this Country.

In this Situation, I could not hesitate as to the Conduct which it became Me to pursue. I have taken the earliest Measures to repel the Aggressions of this hostile Confederacy, and to support those Principles which are elfential to the Maintenance of Our Naval Strength, and which are grounded on the System of Public Law, so longestablished and recognized in Europe.

I have, at the same Time, given such Afl'urances, as manifest My Disposition to renew My ancient Relations with those Powers, whenever it can be done consistently with the Honour of My Crown, and with a just Regard to the Safety of My Subjects. You will, I am perl'uaded, omit nothing on your Part, that can afford Me the most vigorous and effectual Support in My firm Determination to maintain to the utmost, against every Attack, the Naval Rights and the Interests of My Empire.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have directed the Estimates for the several Branches of the Public Service to be laid before you: Deeply as I lament the continued Necessity of adding to the Burdens of My People, I am periuaded you will feel with Me the Importance of providing effectual Means for those Exertions which are indispensibly requilke for the Honour and Security of the Country.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am confident that your Deliberations will be uniformly directed to the great Object of improving the Benefits of that happy Union, which, by the Blessing of Providence, has now been effected; and of promoting, to the utmost, the Prosperity of every Part of My Dominions.

You will, I doubt not, resume the Enquiries which were lo diligently prosecuted in the last Session of Parliament, as to the belt Means of relieving My Subjects from the Pressure of the present high Price of Provisions; and of preventing, as far as it can be done by human Forelight, the Recurrence of similar Difficulties. In these Endeavours, and in every Measure that can contribute to the Happiness of My People, the great End of all My Willies, you may be allured of My cordial Concurrence.

You may rely on My availing Myself of the earliest Opportunity which shall afford a Prol'pest of terminating the present Contest, on Grounds consistent with Our Security and Honour, and with the Maintenance of those elfential Rights on which Our Naval Strength must always principally depend.

It will afford Me the truest and most heartfelt Satisfaction whenever the Disposition of Our Enemies shall enable Me thus to restore to the Subjects of My United Kingdom the Ble flings of Peace, and thereby confirm and augment those Advantages which relult from Our internal Situation, and which, even under all the Difficulties of War, have carried to so great an Extent the Agriculture, Manufactures, Commerce, and Revenue of the Country.

We, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in Parliament aflertibled, b-g Leave to return Your Majesty cur most humble Thanks for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We embrace, with the utmost Satisfaction, the first: Opportunity of humbly testifying to Your Majesty those Sentiments of Duty and Attachment to Your Majesty's Person and Government, and ot Zeal for the Honour of Your Crown and the Interests of Your Dominions, winch will uniformly direct all our Proceedings.

The Advantages resulting from the Accomplishment of that important Measure, by which the prclent vEra is diuinguished, and which is calculated to augment and consolidate the Strength and Relburces of the Empire, and to cement more dolely the Intere [Is and Affections of Your Majesty's Subjects, w ill, we trust, encourage and animate a brave and loyal People to that Vigour, Enctgy, and Firmncfs, which the Circumstances of our prclent Situation so peculiarly require.

The unfortunate Course ot Events on the Continent, and the Consequences which must be expected to re-fult from it, cannot ndeed tail to be Matter G Anxiety and Concern to an who have a just Feeling for the Security and Independence ot Europe-, and it fills us with Astonishment, as well ms Regret, that, at such a Period, any of the Powers of Europe, inttcad ot concerting the Means of mutual Defence against their common and increasing Danger, should lie engaged in Endeavours to weaken the Naval Force of the Empire, which

has hitherto opposed to powerful an Obftacie to the inordinate Ambition of France.

The Disrespect with which the Representations which Your Majesty directed to be made to the Court of Pe-terjburgh, in consequence of the Outrages committed against the Ships, Property, and Persons of Your Subjects, have been treated, and the lubiequent Aifts of Injustice and Violence which have aggravated the Proceedings of which Your Majesty complained, must, we are confident, excite the jull Indignation ot Your Majesty's faithful Subjects; and we feel the indilpcnfi-ble Necefifty of vigorous and effectual Measures to repel the AggrelTions of any Confederacy tomied for the Purpose of establifiling, by Force, a new Code of Maritime Law, inconsistent with the Rights, and hostile to the Interests, of this Country.

We shall look forward, with Earneftncfs, to the first Moment when Your Majesty shall find it practicable to renew the ancient Relations with Powers long in Amity with Your Majesty, confidently with the Ilmour of Your Majesty's Crown, and with a just Regard to the Safety of Your Subjects; but Your Majesty may at all Times rely on our affording You the most vigorous and effectual Support, in a hrm Determination to assert those Principles which are grounded on the System of Public Law so long established and recognized in Europe, and to maintain to the utmost, against every Attack, the Naval Rights and the Interests of the Empire.

We acknowledge, with the utmost Gratitude, Your Majesty's gracious Expressions of the Concern with which Your Majesty observes the continued Necessity of adding to the Burdens of Your People; but, while we sincerely participate in that Sentiment, it is impossible for us not to feel the Importance of providing effectual Means for those Exertions which are indispen-

iibly requisite for the Honour and Security of the

Country.

Permit us to allure Your Majesty, that our Deliberations will be uniformly and diligently directed to the great Object of improving the Benefits of that happy Union, which, by the BlelTing of Providence, has now been effected, and of promoting to the utmost the Prosperity of every Part of Y our Majesty's Dominions.

We shall take the earliest Opportunity to relume the Enquiries prosecuted in the lad Session of Parliament, as to the bed Means of relieving Your Majesty's Sub-jeifts from the P re flu re of the present high Price of Provisions, and of preventing, as far as it can be done by human Forelight, the Recurrence of similar Difficulties.

Impressed with a deep and grateful Sense of Your Majesty's unceaiing Anxiety to contribute to the Hap-pincls of Your People, we have the fulled Reliance on Your Majesty availing Yourself of the earlied Opportunity which shall afford a Prol'peff of terminating the present Conted on Grounds confident with our Security and Honour, and with the Maintenance of those Rights on which our Naval Strength mud always principally depend. And we shall cordially participate with Your Majesty in Sentiments of the trued and most heartfelt Satisfaction, whenever the Dil of our Enemies shall enable Your Majesty thus to redore to the Subjects of Your United Kingdom the Blessings of Peace, and thereby confirm and augment those Advantage? which result from our internal Situation, and which, even under all the Difficulties of War, have carried to so great an Extent the Agriculture, Manufactures, Commerce, and Revenue of the Country.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Thomas Wayth, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Road leading from the Shire Hall, in the Town and Port of Woodbridge, to the broad Street in the Town and Borough of Eye, in the County of Suffolk, is very much out of Repair, narrow, and incommodious for Travellers, and cannot be amended, widened, and kept in Repair, by the ordinary Course of Law: That the said Road passes through a very populous and rich Part of the County of Suffolk, where there are many Corn and Dairy Farms; and, if Powers were given for repairing, widening, and improving the same, it would be of Advantage to all Persons having Occasion to travel thereon, and a considerable Improvement of the several Estates in the Neighbourhood thereof, as well as of Public Utility.

and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed);

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition the said Act was read: And,

Mr. Thomas Bowes being examined, said, That the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed considerable Sums of Money upon the Credit of the Tolls thereby granted; and that notwithstanding the Tolls collected and received, and the Money lo borrowed, have been duly applied and laid out in the repairing and amending of the said Road, yet, by reason of the many heavy Carriages continually passing thereon with Coals, Lime, and Merchandize of divers Kinds, and many of them with narrow Wheels, which cut and tear up the said Road, and the great additional Expence of providing proper Materials for repairing the fame, which are brought from a considerable Distance to many Parts of the said Road, the present Tolls authorized to be taken upon the said Road have been found inadequate to the Repairs thereof, and to keep the same in Repair, and to repay the several Sums of Money borrowed on the Credit of the said Act, unless the Tolls and Powers thereby given be further continued, altered, and enlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill fof continuing and amending an Act, passed in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing the Road from Eorougin the County of York, to the City of Durham; and for more effectually repairing the said Road: And that Mr. Burdon and Mr. Michael Angelo Taylor do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And the Question being again proposed, an Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words " of the United Kingdom of Great Britain " and Ireland."

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting, after the first Word " Parliament," the Words " to concern himself in the " Election."

And the Question being put. That those Words be there inserted;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inserting after the Word " or" the Word " for." .

And the Question being put, That the Word " for" be there inserted;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " to concern themselves in the Elections of Members," and inserting the Words " in that Part of the United " Kingdom called Great Britain, to avail himself of any " Authority derived from his Commission, to influence " the Election of any Member,"

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words in " that Part of the United Kingdom called Great Britain, " to avail himself of any Authority derived from his " Commission, to influence the Election of any Member," be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Persons who will question any Returns of Menv-bers to serve in Parliament for that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, which have been or may be made to Writs already issued, or ordered to be issued, do question the same within Twenty-eight Days after the same thall have been, or shall be, respectively returned into the Crown Office of that Part of the United Kingdom called England.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

An ingrossed Bill to suspend so much of an Act, mk}e in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prevent, until the Sixth Day of November One thousand Eight hundred and One, and from thence " to the End of Six Weeks from the Commencement of " the then next Session of Parliament, the manufacturing " of any Fine Flour from Wheat or other Grain, and " the making of any Bread solely from the Fine Flour of " Wheat; and to repeal an Act, passed in the Thirty-« sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for " permitting Bakers to make and sell certain Sorts of " Bread, and to make more effectual Provision for the " fame," as relates to other Grain than Wheat; and for indemnifying Persons who may have d refled, fold, or used, any Meal or Flour of such other Grain finer than is prescribed by the said Act, was read the third Time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be. An Act to suspend, until the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Eight hundred and One, so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament! inti-9

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That when any such Petition shall have been lodged in the said Office of Clerk of the Crown, in that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, within the Time before limited, the said Clerk shall forthwith make a Copy thereof, to be preserved in the said Office, and immediately thereupon shall transmit such original Petition (in the Method used in conveying Returns of Writs) to the Speaker of the House of Commons, to be by him laid before the House: And that, in case no such Petition shall have been lodged in the said Office within the Time before limited, the said Clerk of the Crown shall forthwith transmit a Certificate in the like Manner to the Speaker of the House of Commons, signed by hini-lelf or his Deputy, specifying the Time when such Return was made, and that no such Petition had been lodged in his Office, previous to the Date of such Certificate.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The House proceeded to take the said Report into further Consideration.

And the First ilelclution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words " Crown Office," and inferring the Words " Office of the Clerk of the Crown " instead thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Words " Crown Office " stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being,put, That the Words " Office of the Clerk of the Crown" be inl'erted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That all Persons who will question any Returns of Members to serve in Parliament for that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, which have been or may be made to Writs already issued, or ordered to be issued, do quest tion the same within Twenty-eight Days after the same shall have been, or shall be respectively returned into the Ollice of the Clerk of the Crown in that Part of the United Kingdom called England.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words " Crown Office, " and inlerting t he Words " Office of the Clerk of the Crown " instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Crown Office " stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words Vol. 56.

" Office of the Clerk of the Crown , K be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended. That all Persons who will question any Returns of Members to serve in Parliament for that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, to Writs not already issued, or ordered to be issued, do question the same by presenting a Petition to this House within Fourteen Days next after the same shall have been brought into the Office of the Clerk of the Crown of that Part of the United Kingdom called England, or by lodging a Petition in the Office of the Clerk of the Crown in that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, within Fourteen Days next after the same shall have been brought into the said Office.

The subsequent Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by inserting after the Words " Office of" the Word " the."

And the Question being put. That the Word " the" be there inserted;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That when any such Petition shall have been lodged in the said Office of the Clerk of the Crown, in that Part of the United Kingdom called Irelanwithin the Time before limited, the said Clerk shall forthwith make a Copy thereof, to be preserved in the said Office, and immediately thereupon shall transmit such original Petition (in the Method used in conveying Returns of Writs) to the Speaker of the House of Commons, to be by him laid before the House: And that, in case no such Petition shall have been lodged in the said Office within the Time before limited, the said Clerk of the Crown shall forthwith transmit a Certificate in the like Manner to the Speaker of the House of Commons, signed by himself or his Deputy, specifying the Time when such Return was made, and that no such Petition had been lodged in his Office previous to the Date of such Certificate.

Ordered, That this House be called over upon this Day Three Weeks, the 2d Day of March next.

Ordered, That such Members as shall not then attend, be sent for in Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

THE House being met, the Clerk at the Table acquainted the House, That he had, this Morning, received a Letter from Mr. Speaker: Which he read to the House j and is as followeth j

Palace Tard,

February the 10th, 1801.

Sir,

His Majesty having been pleased to express His Intention of appointing me, at this Conjuncture, to a Situation which would be incompatible with the Continuance of my Service to the House of Commons, I am obliged to request that you will tender to the House my Resignation of an Office in itself the most honourable, and repeatedly conferred upon me in a Manner the moll gratifying. In quitting such a Situation, endeared to me by Considerations the nearest to my Heart, I am unable adequately to express the Sentiments of Respect, Gratitude, and Regret, with which I am im-prefl'ed; I am sustained by the Consciousness that, on this Occasion, I am actuated by the same Principles of Public Duty, by which it has been my earned Wilh and constant Endeavour to regulate my Conduct, and from which I trull that I shall never deviate.

I am.

With true Regard and Friendship,

Sir,

Your moll obedient Servant, John Ley, Esquire. Henry Addington.

of the Clock in the Afternoon, in the House of Peers, for His Royal Approbation.

Then Mr. Speaker elect put the Question for adjourning the House until Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock; which being agreed to, the House was adjourned accordingly; and Mr. Speaker elect went away; without the Mace before him.

Sir John Honywood reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the City of Canterbury, and County of the same City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, ‘Thomas Hammond, Esquire, down Clerk of the said City, being examined, said, That a Market for the Sale of Live Cattle has, for divers Years lafi: past, been held there, in a certain Piece of Ground situate without the Gate, commonly called Saint George's Gate, belonging to the Corporation, who have at their own Expence maintained the Kails and Pens of the said Cattle Market; that for the Sale of Cattle in the said Market, certain Tolls were formerly paid to the Corporation, but the Payment of such Tolls has been discontinued for a long Time past* And being further examined, he said. That the Market Place is much too imallfor the Number of Cattle usually. brought for Sale; and that, for Want of sufficient and expeditious Means of Punishment, divers ill di/poied Persons frequently destroy the Rails and Pens, to the great Injury of the Market Place, and to the great Costs of the Corporation; that Cattle are frequently expoled to Sale, and negligently and improvidently driven, in the public Streets of the said City, whereby not only, the Persons frequenting the Market, and buying and selling Cattle there, but also the Inhabitants, and all other Persons reforling thereto, are frequently exposed to great Trouble and Danger. And the Witness further laid, That the Corporation have been applied to by many of the Inhabitants of the City, and other Persons frequenting the said Market Place, to enlarge the fame, by adding thereto a Piece of Ground lying contiguous, belonging to the Corporation, in the Occupation of Hannah Mantle, and to erect new and proper Fences and Pens for Cattle, and otherwise to improve the said Market Piace; and have, for that Purpose, offered to pay certain real'onable Tolls to the Corporation f. r the Lioerty of exposing Cattle to Sale in such enlarged and improved Market Place, in Confuleration of the Expence to be incurred in the making and maintaining ot Inch Additions and Improvements. And the Witness added, That the Corporation were willing to comply with such Request, upon receiving a reasonable Recompence for the Ex»

Copy of His Majesty's Commission approving of the Choice of Speaker.

GEORGE R.

GEORGE the Third,by the Grace of God, of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, King, Defender of the Faith. To all to whom these Presents shall come, Greeting. Whereas, We have lately, for divers difficult and pressing Affairs, concerning Us, the State and Defence of Our said United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the Church, ordained this Our present Parliament to begin and to be held at Our City 0 { Westminster,on the Twenty-second Day of

January, in the Forty-first Year of Our Reign, on which Day Our said Parliament was begun and held, and is there now holden. And whereas We have been in-iorrr.ed, that the Lower House of Our said Parliament have lately made Choice of Our Trusty and well-beloved Sir John Mit/ord, Knight, to be Speaker of the said Lower House of Our said Parliament, of which Choice We are graciously pleased to approve, and to allow and confirm the fame, and forasmuch as for divers Causes and Considerations We cannot at this Time conveniently be present in Our Royal Person in Our said Parliament; Know ye, That We, trusting in the Fidelity and Care of Our most dear and entirely beloved Son and most faithful Councillor George Prince of Wales, Our most dear Sons and faithful Councillors Frederick Duke of York, William Duke of Clarence, Edward Duke of Kens, Emeji Duke of Cumberland, the most Reverend Father in God and Our faithful Councillor John Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate and Metropolitan of all England, Our well-beloved and faithful Councillor Alexander Lord Loughborough, Our Chancellor of that Part of Our

United Kingdom called Grea Britain, Our most dear Cousins and Councillors John Earl of Chatham, President of Our Council; John Earl of Keeper

of Our Privy Seal; William Hehry Duke of Portland, One of Our principal Secretaries of State; James Marquis of Salisbury, Chamberlain of Our Household; George Earl of Leicester, Steward of Our Household; Philip Earl of Chesterfield, John Earl of Sandwich, George

John Earl Spencer, John Jeffries Earl Camden, the Right Reverend Father in God and Our faithful Councillor BeilbyLord Bishop of London-, Our well-beloved and faithful Councillors William Wyndham Lord Grenvdlle, One other of Our principal Secretaries of State; George Granville Lord Gower Sutherland, William Shazv Lord Cat he art, Robert Lord Hobart, Thomas Lord,

William Lord Auckland, Welbore Lord George

Lord Macartney, and John Lord Eldon, Chief Justice of Our Court of Common Pleas, by the Tenor of these Presents, do give and grant to them, or any Three or more of them, full Power in Our Name to declare and notify Our Royal Approbation of the Choice of the said Sir' John Mitfordto be Speaker of the said Lower House of

Our said Parliament, and to allow and confirm the said Sir John Mit/ord to be Speaker of the said Lower House, and to do all and every Thing and Things in Our said Parliament that may be necessary for declaring Our said Royal Approbation, Allowance*, and Confirmation of the said Sir John Mitford to be Speaker of the said Lower House of Our said Parliament. In witness whereof We ‘ have caused these Our Letters to be made Patent. Witness Ourself at Westminster, the Twelfth Day of,

in the Forty-first Year of Our Reign.

By the KING Himself,

Signed with His own Hand,

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names art thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others, intended in the Open and Common Fields within the Parish of Littlebury, in the County of Essex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Lands belonging to the Petitioners, and the other Proprietors of the said Open and Common Fields, lie intermixed and dispersed in small Parcels, and are in general inconveniently situated, so as to render the Cultivation thereof difficult and expensive, and, in their present State, are incapable of much Improvement; and it would tend greatly to the Advantage of the said several Proprietors if the same were divided and inclosed, and specific Parts allotted them: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for those Purposes.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Bramston and the Lord Hawkeffury do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being defiroils of conferring a signal Mark of His Favour and Approbation on Captain Sir Sidney Smith, inconsequence of the eminent Services which he has rendered, and the Valour and Ability which he has displayed, during the whole Period of the important Operations, with the Conduct of which he has been entrusted, on the Coast of Egypt, and particularly in the gallant and heroic Defence of the Fortress of recommends it to the House of Commons, to enable His Majesty to make Provision for securing to the said Sir Sidney Smith a Pension of One Thoui'and Pounds per Annum for the Term of his Natural Life,

A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Wilts and Berks Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from the River Thames, or at or near the Town of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, to join or communicate with the Kennet and Avon Canal, at or near the Town of Trowbridge, in the County of Wilts, and also certain Navigable Cuts therein described, certain Persons were incorporated by the Name and Title of " The " Company of Proprietors of the Wilts and Berks Canal Navigation," and were authorized to make, complete, and maintain the said Canal, Cuts, and other Works; and that the Petitioners were, by the said Act, authorized to raise and contribute, among themselves, in Manner therein mentioned, for the Purposes aforesaid, the Sum of £.111,900, which was to be divided into One Thousand One Hundred and Nineteen Shares, of £. 100 each; and, if the same should be found insufficient for the Purposes of the said Act, they were thereby enabled, after the said Sum of £. 111,900 had been raised as aforesaid, to raise and contribute among themselves, or by Mortgage of the Undertaking, in the Manner therein respectively mentioned, a further Sum of £. 150,000, to be applied in carrying the several Purposes of the said Act into Execution, but they have only been able to raise the Sum of £.61,512. or. 10 or thereabouts, as only the Sum of £.74,100, Part of the said Sum of £.111,900, amounting to Seven Hundred and Forty-one Shares, of £.100 each, was originally subscribed, and the Petitioners are indebted to their Treasurer in the Sum of £.3,796. 15 s.7 advanced by him, for which they have engaged to pay him Interest, which, together with the said Sum of £.61,512. or. 10 so raised as aforesaid, has been duly applied, but is found to be very insufficient for the Purposes of carrying on and completing the said Undertaking, and the Petitioners have also incurred sundry other Debts, which are yet due and owing by them; and that the Petitioners have proceeded in making certain Parts of the said Canal, Cuts, and other Works, but will not be able to complete the said Undertaking unless they are enabled and authorized to raise more Money for that Purpose, and for discharging their said Debts; and that the Petitioners have, in proceeding to carry the said Act into Execution, found the Powers and Provisions thereof, in several Respedls, defective, and it is expedient that the same should be altered and amended; and that it is also expedient to ascertain and fix the Termination of the said Canal at the West End thereof, and also the Terminations of the Two Cuts or Branches to be made from the said Canal to the Towns of Chippenham and Caine, in the said Acts particularly mentioned: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the

A Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and others, of the Vestry of the Township of Dewsbury, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That it is with deep Concern they find themselves under the Necessity of representing to the House, that, owing to the sudden Decline of Trade, the extraordinary high Price of Provisions, and the Increase of Inhabitants, within the said Township, they are extremely oppressed, and Numbers of them reduced to great Distress, on account of their principal Manufacturers being obliged to dismiss a very large Proportion of their Workmen, and their lesser Manufacturers, daily sinking from a State of industrious Prosperity to Indigence, are now chiefly supported by Parochial Relief; in consequence whereof, their Poor Rates have advanced to such an alarming Height, that the Inhabitants of the said Township are utterly incapable of supporting the Pressure: — That within the said Township there are only Nine Hundred and Seventy-three Acres of inclosed Land, including the Wood Lands, and no Common Open Town Fields, the Rack Rents of which do not exceed £.2,250 and the Rack Rents of the Houses (a large Proportion of the Occupiers of which are not able to pay either Rent or Taxes) do not exceed £.3,500 per Year; and that the Poor Rates for the last Ten Years have been as follows; viz. for the Year 1790, £.396. 17 3

The Right honourable Henry Addington being come Mr. Adding-to the House, Mr. Speaker acquainted him, that the ton tlunkcd* House had, Y'efterday, unanimously resolved, That the Thanks of this House be express'ed, in the strongest Terms, to the Right honourable Henry Addington, for ' the exemplary and distinguished Manner in which he discharged the Duties of Speaker during the Whole of the Period in which he tilled the Chair of the House of Commons: That he be allured, that the Proofs which he has uniformly given of Attachment to the Constitution, the Steadiness with which he has maintained the Dignity and Privileges of this House, the Ability, Integrity, and unremitting Attention to Parliamentary Business, which have marked the Whole of his Conduct, justly entitle him to our Approbation, Respect, and Gratitude: And Mr. Speaker gave him the Thanks of the House accordingly; as followeth;

Mr. Addington,

The House have unanimously resolved, That the Thanks of this House be express'ed in the strongest Terms to you, Sir, for the exemplary and distinguished Manner in which you discharged the Duties of Speaker during the Whole of the Period in which you filled the Chair of the House of Commons: That you be allured that the Proofs which you have uniformly given of Attachment to the Constitution, the Steadiness with which you have maintained the Dignity and Privileges of this House, the Ability, Integrity, and unremitting Attention to Parliamentary Business, which have marked the Whole of your Conduct, justly entitle you to their Approbation, Respect, and Gratitude; and it is my Duty to convey to you the Thanks of the House, according to this Resolution. In Discharge of this Duty, if I were to indulge my private Feelings, I should easily find Topics on which to expatiate. But lam to thank you for your Conduct in this Chair, and on that Subject the Resolution itself amply conveys the Opinion of the House. If I were to endeavour to give their Sentiments in other Words, I should probably only weaken the Force of the Expressions which they have used; and I will not therefore attempt to convey to you their Thanks in any Language but their own.

Upon which Mr. Addington said,

Mr. Speaker,

It is with Sensations of the most respe&ful, and heart- Mr. Adding-felt, Gratitude, that I receive the Testimony of Appro- ton* bation, which you have communicated to me, in Obedi-

fence to the Commands of the House. To enjoy their good Opinion was my Pride, and Comfort, during my Continuance in their Service; to experience such a Proof of it, as has been afforded me upon the present Occasion, is indeed the highest Honour, and the most gratifying Reward. Being only conlcious of having discharged my Duty with Zeal, and Fidelity, I feel a Satisfaction, which I am unable to express, in being allowed to indulge the Hope, that the Chair, in which you preside, has not loft, by my Conduct, any Portion of that Dignity, and Authority, which are so. essential to the well-regulated Freedom of Debate, as well as to the Rights and Privileges of the Representatives of the People, and which you, Sir, I am sure, will ever be disposed to maintain. My best Acknowledgments, Sir, are due to you, for the Manner in which you have been pleased to execute the Orders of the House: To the House itself I owe every Obligation, which can bind the Duty, Veneration, and Attachment of an Individual to the first Public Body in the World.

That every Contributor shall, on or before the 20th Day of this Instant February, make a Deposit of £. 10. per Centum on such Sum as he or she shall chuse to fub-scribe, towards raising the said Sum of Twenty-eight Millions, with the Chief Cashier or Cashiers of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, as a Security for making the future Payments on or before the Days or Times herein after mentioned; that is to lay;

That all the Monies so to be received by the said Cashier or Cashiers of the said Governor and Company of the Bank of England shall be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, to be applied, from Time to Time, to such Services for Great Britain and Ireland, as shall then have been voted by this House in this Session of Parliament:

That every Contributor, who shall pay in the Whole of his or her Contribution Money towards the said Sum of Twenty-eight Millions, at any Time on or before the 13th Day of October 1801, shall be allowed an Interest, by Way of Discount, after the Rate of £. per Centum per Annum, on the Sum so advanced for completing his or her Contribution respectively, to be computed from the Day of completing the same to the nth Day of December 1801.

Mr. Wilberforce reported from the Committee, to Sculcoates whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names ^reported! are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the Parish of Sculcoates, in the East Riding of the County of York, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Paving Bills, had been complied with j and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House} and he read the Report in his Place} and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read} and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Stephen Dickinson being examined, said. That the Parish of Sculcoates is a Place of very large Extent, and that a very extensive Trade is carried on there; that the several Streets, Squares, Lanes, Ways, Passages, and public Places already made and built, and which are now making and building within the said Parish, are in many Parts incommodious and unsafe for Passengers, very ill paved, and not sufficiently cleansed, lighted, and watched, and are subject to various Nuisances, Annoyances, Encroachments, and Obstructions, and that the o^her Streets and public Places, intended to be made or built, may become liable to the same Inconveniences: that it would tend greatly to the Convenience, Benefit, and Safety of the Public, as well as of the Owners and Inhabitants of Houses which are or may be built within the said Parish, and to all Persons resorting to or passing through the fame, if such Streets and other public Places were properly payed, cleansed, lighted, watched, and regulated, and all Nuisances, Annoyances, Encroachments, and Obstructions removed and prevented for the future: And the Witness added. That it would also tend to the Convenience and Benefit of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, and to the Public, if a sufficient Number of Hackney Coaches and Chairs, and of Porters, Coal Carriers, and Water Carriers, Trucks, Carts, land other Carriages, were licensed, and put under proper Regulations.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for paving, cleansing, lighting, watching, and regulating, the Streets, Squares, Lanes, and other public Passages and Places, within the Parish of Sculcoates, in the East Riding of the County of York j and for removing and preventing Nuisances, Annoyances, Encroachments, and Obstructions} and for licensing and regulating Hackney Coaches, Chairs, Porters, Coal Carriers, and Water Carriers, Trucks, Carts, and other Carriages, within the said Parish: And that Mr. Wilberforce and Mr. Henry Lascelles do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Bragge reported from the Committee, appointed Second Re-to take into Consideration what additional Orders, and what other Regulations, it may be proper to make re- orders' relative to the Proceedings of this House in consequence spefting Ire-of the Union of Great Britain and Ireland, and to report the fame, together with their'Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House, That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had come to several other Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House -, and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as fohoweth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Peer of Ireland, unleis actually elected and l'ery-ingfor any County, City, or Borough, of Great Britain, hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to l'erve in Parliament for that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Peer of Ireland, elected (or w ho shall be elected) to lit and vote on the Part of Ireland in the House of Lords of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, of who hath, or shall have, voted at such Election, hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to ierve in Parliament for that Part of the United Kingdom called Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons, for any Lord of Parliament to concern himself in the Election, or for any Governor of any County in that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, to avail himself of any Authority derived from his Commission to influence the Election of any Mem- ber to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the 39th and 40th Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for reducing, until the First Day of June One " thousand F.ighr hundred, the Duties upon Spirits " distilled from Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture " therewith, for prohibiting the Distillation of Spirits " from Wheat or Wheat Flour, and for reducing, until the Twentieth Day of September One thousand Fight hundred, and better collecting, the Duties " payable on the Importation of Starch," as relates to the reducing and bet ter collecting the Duties payable on the Importation of Starch, which was, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, revived, amended, and further continued until the Expiration of Six Weeks after the

Commencement of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 37th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act authorizing " His Majesty, for a limited Time, to make Regulations respecting the Trade and Commerce to and from " the Cape of Good Hope," which was by Four Acts, of the 38th, 39th, and 40th Y'ears of the Reign of His present Majesty, and by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, further continued until the Expiration of Six Weeks after the Commencement of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 33d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for " better preventing Offences in obstructing, destroying, " or damaging, Ships or other Velfeis, and in obstructing Seamen, Keel men, Callers, and Ship Carpenters, " from pursuing their lawful Occupations," which was to continue in force until the 24th Day of June 1800, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which was, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, continued until the Expiration of Six Weeks after the Commencement of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be made perpetual.

Mr. Ryder accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Rdblutions which the Committee had di-rested to be reported to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's 1 able: Where the same were read j and are as followeth; viz, »

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be given on every Barrel of Superfine Wheaten Flour, of One Hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight, which shall be imported into Great Britain in any Ship which shall have cleared out from any Port in America, between the 12th Day of November 1800 and the iotli Day of Jamuny 1801, and shall be sold by Public Sale by Auction within Two Months after Importation, a Bounty equal to the Sum by which the actual Price of each Barrel of such Flour so fold shall be less than Eighty Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be given on every Barrel of Fine Wheaten Flour, of One Hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight, which shall be imported into Great Britain in any Ship which shall have cleared out from any Port in America, between the 12th Day of Novem 1 Soo and the 10th Day of January 1801, and shall be sold by Public Sale by Auction within Two Months after Importation, a Bounty equal to the Sum by which the actual Price of each Barrel of such Flour lo fold shall be less than Seventy-eight Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be given on every Barrel of Superfine Wheaten Flour, of One Hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight, which shall be imported into Great Britain in any Ship which shall have cleared out from any Port in America, between the 10th Day of January 1801 and the 25th Day of March 1801, and shall be sold by Public Sale by Auction within Two Months after Importation, a Bounty equal to the Sum by which the actual Price of each Barrel of such Flour so fold shall be less than Ninety Shillings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be given on every Barrel of Fine Flour, of One Hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Weight, which shall be imported into Great Britain in any Ship which shall have cleared out from any Port in America, between the 10th Day of January and the 25th Day of March 1801, and shall be sold by Public Sale by Auction within Two Months after Importation, a Bounty equal to the Sum by which the actual Price of each Barrel of such Flour so fold shall be less than Eighty-eight Shillings.

A Petition of the Churchwardens and Overseers of Petition from the Poor of Fourteen Townships within the Parishes'of Halifax and Bradford, in the West Riding of the County speaing the of York, was presented to the House, and read; Set- Poor Rate,« ting forth. That the Petitioners are reduced to the extremeft Difficulties by the extraordinary Pressure of the Times, which renders them incapable of supporting their Poor, or even so far administering towards the same as to preserve them in Existence; that they are nearly naked, which is a most lamentable Thing at this Season of the Year, especially in that cold Part of the Kingdom; to remedy this is not in the Power of the Parish Officers, on account of the Inadequacy of their present Funds; that the Number of Paupers in the said Townships has increased beyond all former Calculation since the ift of December last, and they are daily flocking in great Numbers to the Petitioners, from the general Want of Employment occasioned by the great and alarming Stoppage of our Manufactories, which Affliction being greatly aggravated by the exorbitant Price of Provisions, causes hourly Distress, at which Humanity Ihudders, and of which the Petitioners can no longer be Eye Witnesses without laying the same before the House: — That by far the major Part of those paying Assessments are in Distress nearly equal to the Paupers themselves, occasioned by the present Dearnels of Provisions, reduced State of their Manufactories, low Wages, and almost total Want of Employment; and farther, the Petitioners are in very heavy Advances of Money for their several Townships, and every AC-leflment they lay very greatly tends to increase the Number of their Poor; add to which, the Deficiencies in the Collection of the present Poor Rates in the said Townships are large, and increasing, and the Debt of each is very considerable: Under these Circumstances, the Petitioners pray the House will grant such immediate Assistance as will enable them to relieve their Poor in an equal Degree with Leeds, Wakefield,

and other more opulent Places, in the West Riding of the County of York,which, at present, give triple the Sum to their Poor that the present reduced State of Funds of the Petitioners enable them to give theirs in similar Circumstances; and without which, they allure the House, that the Poor, of the said Townships cannot polfibly exist much longer.

mined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills* had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Knocker being examined, said. That the Road leading from Dovor to Sandwich, by in the County of Kent, through the several Parishes mentioned in the Petition, is very much out of Repair, and in many Places narrow, circuitous, and incommodious; and by Reason of many sudden Turnings, and of the Number of Carriages daily passing thereon, the said Road is in many Parts very ruinous and unsafe, and the Inhabitants of the said several Parishes have not the Means of amending the same, although they have regularly performed their Statute Duty thereon: — That the Improvement of the said Road will be of great public Utility and Convenience, and is particularly necessary to the Trade of that Part of the Country, both f6r the transport of Timber and of Com, Dovor being a Port of extensive Trade in the Line of Shipbuilding, and wherein a principal Part of the Boats for the Navy have been accustomed to be built; and there being not less than Eleven Mills in the Distance of Three Miles on a Stream running to Dovor, and the Public, particularly the Farmers, Boat Builders, and Millers, from the Badness of the Roads, not being able to draw their very necessary Articles from that Part of the Country, but on the most disadvantageous Terms. — And the Witness further said, That a great Part of the present Road might be very considerably widened, altered, and improved, so as to make it safe and commodious to Carriages and Passengers, and considerable and advantageous new Lines of Road might be formed through the several Parishes described in the Petition, and thereby several sudden Turnings and narrow Places would be avoided, and the Distance of the Road from Dovor to Sandwich, by Walderjhare, considerably short-cned and improved.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for altering, widening, and repairing the Road leading from the Town and Port of Dovor to the Town and Port of Sandwich, through the Parish of Walderjhare, and also the Road from the present Turnpike Road leading from Dovor to Barham Downs, up Kerfney Court Hill, to the Parish of Whitfield otherwise Beausfield, in the County of Kent: And that Sir Edward Knatchbull, Mr. nion. The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for relieving certain Persons from the; Payment of the Poor Rates, and for extending Parochial Relief, in certain Cafes, for a Time to be limited;

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint George the Martyr, in Southwark, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners conceive that, by the present Poor Laws, all the Powers intended to be granted to the Justices of the Peace by the said Bill, are now vested in, or exercised by, the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the different Parishes in England, who, from their local Situation, and the Knowledge which they have of the Characters and Situations of the Persons in their different Parishes applying to be excused from Payment of the Poor Rates, must necessarily be better enabled to determine on their Cafes than a Justice of the Peace residing, and acting out of, and at a Distance from, such Parish; and that in the ParilH of Saint George, Southwark, which is extensive, and contains near 5,000 Houses, the far greater Number of which are of very small Annual Value, there is not a Angle residing acting Justice, and the Whole of the Parochial Business of that and all the other Parishes in the Borough of Southwark, and Eastern Half of the Hundred of Brixton, in the County of Surrey, is performed by the Police Justices at Union Southwark, who have already heaped upon them an infinite Variety of Business; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, it would be utterly impossible for the Magistrates at that Office, with the most active Exertions, to do Justice to the numerous Applications for Relief from Payment of the Poor Rates under the present Bill, if passed into a Law, because it would be impossible for them personally to enquire into the individual Cafes of the Persons applying from the several Parishes within their extensive and populous District; and that the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the Parish of Saint George the Martyr are in the daily Practice of relieving very many of the Housekeepers within the Parish, whose Situation and Circumstances render such Relief neccfi'ary, from the Payment of the Poor Rates; that they fit Weekly for that Purpose, and the Petitioners are convinced that they do this with more Discrimination and Justice than any other Description of Persons could do; and that no one is ever fumtnoned for the Payment of a Poor Rate until one or more of the Churchwardens or Overseers have full actually visited the House of the Individual, seen the Situation of the Family, and enquired into its Circumstances; and the Petitioners are informed, and believe, that a similar Mode is followed by almost all the Parish Officers in and about the Metropolis; and that in the said Parish, from its particular

local

Order for Committee oil Bill to relieve certain Persons from the Poor Rates, read.

Petitipil from Southwark* against B* Bill.

local Situation, the Bill alluded to, if passed, would be productive of great injustice, by throwing the Payment of the principal Part of the Poor Rates upon the Shopkeepers, very many of whom are in very distressed Circumstances, but who, from the Nature of their Calling, are obliged to live in or near the principal Street, and to pay very exorbitant Rents, whilst Numbers of Persons, in much easier and more affluent Circumstances, reside in small Houses, which are very low rented, in Saint George's Fields, and its Neighbourhood; and that the Petitioners conceive that the said Bill, if palfcd into a Law, will be very prejudicial to the Morals of the People, particularly in Cities and great Towns, by the Multiplication of Oaths, and by making the Relief principally depend upon the Oath of the Party applying, which will operate as a Bribe for the Commission of Perjury by idle and profligate Persons, whilst: the honest, industrious, really distrelied, but modest Man, will perhaps sooner luster any Inconvenience than expose himself by appearing in a Public Hall, and openly (wearing to his Inability to discharge his Assessment, who, however, at present, frequently finds-Relief from the Parish Officers, without a Public Exposure of his Circumstances; and that the Petitioners, upon Principle, and without any particular Allulion, cannot but remark, that the Bill, if passed, will, in their Opinion, materially affect the Freedom of Election in open and populous Towns and Boroughs, and particularly within the Environs of the Metropolis, by investing the Justices, who are appointed by and under the immediate Patronage of the executive Servants of the Crown, with a large Power and Influence over great Numbers of Individuals possessing Votes, and who happen to be in the Situation intended to be benefited by the proposed Bill, and whose Franchises, the Bill expressly enacts, shall not be affcdled by such Relief: And therefore, for these Reasons, praying, That the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And a Motion was made, and the Question being put. That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair $

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Right honourable Lord Napier informed your Committee, That the Laws now lubfifting in Scotland, for making of Roads, have been found ineffectual in the County of Selkirk, and other and further Powers are necessary, in order to carry the Purposes of the said Laws into Execution; and Doubts have arisen, in some Cafes, who are chargeable towards repairing the Highways; and it is attended with Difficulty and Trouble, to make effectual, and properly apply, the Statute Work in the said County: — That a reasonable Composition in Money, instead of Labour, is, in many Places, found to be more useful and effectual for the Purpose of making and repairing the Roads, as well as more easy and convenient for the Persons liable in Statute Services, than the actual Performance of the fame; and it will be of Advantage to the said County to convert the Services into Money, and ascertain the Rates and Mode of levying the fame.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred, to consider of so much of an Act, passed in the 38th Year of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act. " for repealing the Duties upon Male Servants, Carriages, Horses, Mules, and Dogs; and for granting to " His Majesty other Duties in lieu thereof," as charges a Duty on Horses kept and used for the Purposes of Husbandry, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed:; viz.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person, occupying a Farm, the Rack Rent of which shall be less than Twenty Pounds a Year, and making a Livelihood solely thereby, or occupying any other Estate on any Tenure, otherwise than as Tenant, at Rack Rent, or such other Estate, together with a Farm, at Rack Rent, the Value of which, in the Whole, shall be less than equivalent to a Farm, at the Rack Rent of Twenty Pounds a Year, (reckoning the Value of every Estate, occupied by the Owner thereof, on any Tenure except at Rack Rent, as equivalent to Double the like Amount of any Farm at Rack Rent) and making a livelihood solely by such Occupation, and keeping not more than Two Horses, Mares, Geldings, or Mules, in the Whole, shall be chargeable with any of the Duties imposed by the said Act, for, or in respect of, such Horles, Mares, Geldings, or Mules, provided such Horses, Mares, Geldings, or Mules, be bond side kept and used for the Purposes of Husbandry.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, an Amendment was proposed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Word "Twenty," and inserting the Word " Fifty," instead thereof.
