A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Port of Hythe, in the County of Kent, and of the Gentlemen, Hythe, against Farmers, and others, of the adjoining Neighbourhood, I>°vw and whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to g^6 Ro*"* the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Year 1764, an Act was made for explaining an Act therein mentioned, and for amending, widening, and repairing, the Road leading from Cowgate and Archcliff Fort, in Dover, through Folkstone, to the Town of Hythe, in the said County; and that by a Clause therein, the Trustees are empowered to erfift Turnpike Gates between the Town of Dover and the Town of Folkstone only; and that the Petitioners are informed a Bill is depending in the House for enlarging the Term, and altering the Powers, of the said Acts, wherein it is proposed not only to omit the before-mentioned restraining Clause, but to insert therein a Clause for erecting a Gate between Hythe and Seabrook, which is a Distance of a Mile and a Half from Hythe, as good almost as any Road in the Kingdom, and leads on the North to a very exrenfive Country, almost equal in Traffic to the Road which leads on to

Dover,

4i Geo. III.

Dover, and many of the Petitioners residing to the North of such Road, as well as the Inhabitants of (where near One hundred Houses have been built in the last Thirty Years) conceive it will be a great Hardship upon them to pay a Toll for travelling so short a Distance on so good a Road, especially as Five Miles of the Road between Dover and Foil]?one, upon which almost the Whole of the Debt has been incurred, is free from any Gate whatever; and that the present Tolls, and the proposed Increase thereof, would, with proper Management, be fully equal to keep the Road in Question in very complete Repair; and that the Road from to

Hythe is now' very good, and requires no other Repair than what the Parishes in which the same lies will give it; and it would be a manifdl Injury and Hardship to those Places, and to the Inhabitants of the lurrounding Country, if the Clause propolcd should (land Part of the intended Bill, or if any Gate should be erected between Sandgate and Hythe :And therefore praying the House, not to permit the Clause for erecting a Gate between Seabrook and Hythe, to (land Part of the proposed Bill, but to increase the Tolls, as before mentioned, upon the present Gate, and to continue the Clause in the existing Act, for restraining the Erection of Gates, to the Road between Dover and Folkjione, or at lead between Dover and Sandgate;or that the House will confine the Powers of the Act to the latter Distance, and leave the Three Miles from thence to Hythe, out of the proposed Bill, and let them be repaired, as they have hitherto been done, by the Parishes in which they lie; and that the House will give such further and other Relief to the Petitioners as shall seem meet; and that the Petitioners may be heard, by their Counsel or Agents, against such Parts of the said Bill, as affedt their Rights and Interests.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Conficlcration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term, and altering the Powers, of Tw'O Acts, one made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the other made in the 4th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending, widening, and repairing, the Roads leading from Dover to Barham Downs, and from Cowgate and ArchciiJ Fort, in Dover, through Folkjione, to the Town of Hythe, in the County of Kent, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel or Agents, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

John Clevland, Esquire, a Member present, informed the Committee, That the above was the Receipt signed by him on the 13th Instant, in the Evening. On Monday the 16th, he put the Writ up himself in a Parcel, and directed it to Mr. Heale, at Exeter, dated the 16th, Carriage paid: That he had previously written by that Day's Post to Mr. Heale, to get it from the Mail, and to forward it immediately to Mr. Mallet, who is appointed by the Court of Chancery, Receiver of Lord Clinton's Estate, and who relides at Toning!on: That he had also written to Mr. Mallet, (which Letter was inclosed in the same Parcel with the Writ) to carry it himself to the High Sheriff of Cornwall; but, if he was not able to go himself, as being ill of the Gout, to fend his Nephew, John Mallet,with the Writ to the High Sheriff', or his

Deputy, and to wait till he had made out the Precept, and to carry it to the Returning Officer of Callington: That having so made up the Parcel, lie delivered it to John Cure, his Servant, with Directions to carry it to the Exeter Mail Coach Office, (the Coffee House)

with Orders to take a Receipt, and fee it booked: That on the Sen'ant's Return, he produced a Receipt in the following Words

" Mr. Heale,

" St. David's Hill,

' " Car. Paid, " Exeter.

" 16th March 1801, "

Exeter Mail."

That he (Mr. Clevland) growing uneasy at not hearing of the Receipt of the Writ, he wrote to the aforesaid Mr. Heale, on Thursdaythe 19th, to enquire into the Causes of the Delay: That on the 21st he received a Letter from Mr. Heale,dated Exeter, March 19th, in the following Words:

" HonJ Sir,

" I was favoured with your's on Wednesday Morning " 17th Instant. I immediately made Enquiries for the " Parcel, but none was come by the Mail, or any Coach, " neither was there any Thing by last Night's Mail; but, " if any Thing arrives, I will forward it immediately, accordingly to your llequest."

That on the 24th, he (Mr. Clevland) received another Letter from Mr. Heale, dated Exon, 22d March, in the following Words:

" Hon4 Sir,

" In Answer to your Letter of the 20th Instant, I " have to inform you, I answered your Letter of the " 16th Instant, by Friday's Post, which you ought to " have Saturday; wherein I informed you, that no " Parcel had arrived for me by Mail Coach on " Tuesday Night or Wednesday Night, and have made " strict Enquiry every Night. Nothing has come to " Hand but a Parcel for Mr. Drake, which I

" forwarded by the Post Boy on Saturday last. I have " been this Morning and examined the Weigh Bills, and Books of Accounts, for all Parcels sent by Coach, but " nothing in my Name to be found: you will make " Enquiry of the Person you sent with it to the Coach " Office in London."

That he (Mr. Clevland) being informed by the Bookkeeper of the Coach Office, that this Mail went through Bath, he wrote to Doctor Merry, Physician at Bath, to make Enquiry for the Parcel containing the Writ,

there. That he has received Two Letters, dated the 26th. and 27th Instant, from Doctor Merry, Hating, that he had made Enquiries at the Inn where the Exeter Mail Hops, but could get no Intelligence of the Weigh Bill, which was stated to be forwarded to Exeter: That from all these Circumstances, he (Mr. Clevland) apprehends the Parcel containing the Writ, must be loft.

i Book produced, and Entry read as follows:

" Monday 16th March 1801. "P. P. Mr. Heale, Exeter. 4

What became of the Parcel ? ----- -It was delivered to

be sent by the Exeter Coach which goes through Bath.

Is not a Weigh Bill made out of all Parcels sent by the Coach? ----- -There is.

Where is the Weigh Bill of that Night's Mail ? ——

It is kept at Thatcham, in Berkshire.

Which of the Servants belonging to the Coach, has the Charge of delivering Parcels directed to Exeter ?

----- If they arrive fafeat Bath, they are then entered on

another Weigh Bill, to be forwarded to Exeter.

How will it appear that they arrive fiife at Bath ?---

In the first place, if the Parcel is missing when the Coach comes to Thatcham, or Bath, it will be marked as such on the Weigh Bill, and, of course, will not be entered in the new Weigh Bill to

Where is the Weigh Bill from Thatcham to Bath ?

----- That is the Weigh Bill to which I have before

referred, and which is at Thatcham.

Have you made any Enquiries about this Parcel ? -

I have written twice to Mr. Phillips at the Hotel, Exeter, but have received no Answer: I might have received an Answer to the last by this Day's Post. I all'o wrote to Mr. Dover, Lamb Inn, Bath, on Wednesday Evening the 25th, but have received no Answer.

Are you sure by which of the Exeter Mails the Parcel

went by? ----- --1 have every Reason to believe that it

went by the Exeter Mail which goes through Bath.

Mr. Clevland produced to the Committee, a Letter which he received this Day from Mr. Heale, dated Exeter, 28th March, by which it appeared,

That he had not then received the said Parcel; and that he had examined the Weigh Bills of all the Coaches that go from London and Exeter, from the 16th to the 26th, and could find no Entry of such a Parcel.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Leeds and Mr. Pepys:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, passed in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the City of Peterborough, through Oundle and Thrapston, to Wellingborough, in the County of Northampton, and for repairing and widening several other Roads near or adjoining thereto; without any Amendment: and also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Wastes, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, within the Parish of Littlebury, in the County of Essex; with some Amendments j to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act

allotting, and inclosing, the Whole Year

Lands, Common Fields, Half Year or Shack Lands, Commonable Grounds, Lammas Meadows, Whin Lots or Doles, Heaths, Commons, and Waste Lands, within the Parish of Great Creffmgham, in the County of Norfolk, and certain open and inclosed Fields, and Half Year or Shack Lands, Meadows, and Pastures, lying in the said Parish, and in the Parish of Little Crejfing/iam, in the said County; with an Amendment; to which Amendment the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Aleans for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Refblutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied such Part of the Aids or Supplies granted by the Parliament of that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, for the Service of the Year ending at Lady Day One thousand Eight hundred and One, as shall exceed the Proportion of the said Aids or Supplies, from the 25th Day of March 1800, to the ill Day of January 1801.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable on Tea, imported into that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, do ceal'e and determine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there shall be paid upon all Tea imported into that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, the Duties following; that is to say, if such Tea shall have been purchased at any Sale or Sales of the East India Company in,

at a Price not exceeding Two Shillings and Six Pence, British,per Pound Weight, a Duty ot Twenty Pounds, Irish currency, per Centum on such Price; and, if such Tea shall have been purchased as aforesaid, at a Price exceeding Two Shillings and Six Pence, British, per Pound Weight, a Duty of Thirty-five Pounds, Currency, per Centum on such Price.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, there shall be paid on all Alufcovado, or Clayed Sugar, imported into that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, an additional Duty of Two Shillings, Irift Currency, for every Hundred Weight thereof, containing One Hundred and Twelve Pounds.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there shall be levied and paid for and upon every Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, of all Sugar, called Bartards, White, or Ground, being of the Manufacture of Britain, and imported directly from thence into that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, an additional Duty of Two Shillings, Irish Currency.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, there shall be levied and paid for and upon ever}- Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, of all Sugar, called Lumps, being of the Manufacture of Great Britain, and imported directly from thence into that Part of the United Kingdom, called Ireland, an additional Duty of Three Shillings and Nine Pence, Irish Currency.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Seven Hundred and One Thousand Two Hundred and Fifty Pounds be raised by Way, of Lottery, such Lottery to consist of Fifty Thousand Tickets, at Fourteen Pounds and Six Pence each; and that the Contributors towards the same shall, on or before the 10th Day of this Instant dpril make a Deposit with the Caftiier of the Bank of England of One Pound and Six Pence, in respect of the Monies to be paid for every such Ticket, as a Security for making the tuture Payments to the said Cashier on or before the Times herein after limited; that is to say,

Mr. Hawkins Browne reported from the Committee, appointed to consider of the present High Price of Provisions, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof, together with several Resolutions thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That none of the Money to be advanced upon Loan to Von. 56.

Parishes, or Townships, shall be granted, unless where the Commissioners are satisfied that the Parish, or Township, applying for Relief, is absolutely unable to prevent extreme Distress, without some Assistance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the intended Relief should be confined to Parishes and Places, in which the Total Produce of the Rate, levied for the Year ending at Easter 1801, shall have exceeded considerably the Produce of the Rate for the Year ending at Easter 1800; and that no greater Slim be advanced for Relief in the Current Quarter, than Three Fourths of the Sum by which the Sum expended in the Relief of the Poor, in the Quarter immediately preceding, exceeded the Sum expended in the Quarter ending at Easter 1800; but, that a Power ought to be given to depart frorfl the Rules contained in this Resolution, in extraordinary Cafes, which will not admit of an Adherence to them; provided nevertheless, that such Departure never takes place without the Reasons on which it is founded being regularly recorded in Writing, by those who have the Management of the Fund, out of which Relief is to be granted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, praying for Relief on the Behalf of any Parish, or Township, should be required to prepare a Statement, setting forth the Amount of the Rental, according to which the Poors Rate is levied, specifying whether that Rate is levied on the full Rack Rent, and, if not, specifying what Proportion the Rental on which that Rate is raised, bears to the full Rack Rent; also, setting forth the Sums raised by the Poors Rate in each of the Five last Years, and in the last Quarter immediately preceding the Application for Relief, and in the Quarter ending at Easter 1800; also the Increase of the Number of the Poor, and the Decrease of the Number of those who have actually paid to the Rates in the course of the last Year, compared with the preceding Year, the Reasons of the Decrease of the Number of those who pay to the Rates, the Nature of the Employments followed by the different Descriptions of the Poor, and the Degree in which the Poor are able to obtain Employment, and, if employed, whether their Earnings are dimini(he4 or increased, and in what Proportion; and that fuqh Statements should be subscribed by Two of His Majesty's Justices of the Peace in the Neighbourhood, declaring, under their Signatures, that they believe the Statements to be true; and that the respective Parishes, or Townships, are absolutely unable to prevent extreme Distress by any legal Measures in their Power; and that thf Statements so subscribed, should be sent, together with such Observations and Explanations, as such Justices may think it right to give, to the Lords of His Majesty's Treasury, or to such Commissioners as they may apppoint, for receiving the fame; and that such Lords of the Treasury, or Commissioners, should be empowered to require from the said Overseers and Churchwardens, or Justices, any further Information they may think requisite, and to advance such Sums to the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of those several Parishes and Townships, which, in their Judgment, ought to be relieved, as shall appear to them requisite and advisable, and confident with the former Resolution relative to the Amount of Relief to be granted. '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, or One of them, should give Vouchers for the Sums so received, and that the said Sums should be repaid by the Parishes receiving the same respectively, by Ten Half Yearly Instalments, the First Instalment to be paid at Lady Day 1804, at furthest; and that the Instalments for repaying the said Sums, should be raised like the Poors Rate, by a proportionate Levy on those who pay to that Rate in each Parish, or Township; and

Report re Burdon reported from the Committee, appointed spe&ingRoads *° consider of the Standing Orders of the House, relative in indoiure to Bills of Inclosure, so far as respects the setting out or the altering of public Roads, and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had examined into the Matters to them referred, and had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Bills for Inclosures, there be inserted a Clause, by which the Commissioners shall be required to set out the public Roads and Highways in such Directions, as shall, upon the Whole, appear to them most commodious for the Public, and to give Notice of the general Lines of such intended Roads, in some one Newspaper of the County, or, if there is no such Paper printed in that County, then in the Newspaper of some near or adjoining County, as soon as may be after the setting out of such Roads, appointing, in the same Notice, a Meeting of the Commissioners, to be held at some convenient Place in, or near to, the Parish or Township within which the Inclosures are to be made, and not sooner than Ten Days from the giving such Notice; at which Meeting, any Person or Persons, who may be dissatisfied with the setting out of the said public Roads and Highways, may attend, to state to the said Commissioners his or their Objections, who shall be required to hear and examine such Objections} and if the said Commissioners, at their said Meeting, shall refuse to alter the said public Road or Roads, or Highways, (to which Objections shall have been stated) to the Satisfaction of the Person or Persons objecting thereto, then the Person or Persons so dissatisfied shall be entitled to appeal against all or any of such public Roads or Highways, to some General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the County, within Four Calendar Months next after such Meeting of the Commissioners as aforesaid, giving Notice, in Writing, to such Commissioners, of the Intention to appeal within Ten Days after such Meeting, and entering into Recognizance, with sufficient Sureties, before a Justice of the Peace for the said County, to try the said Appeal; and that the said Commissioners, or One of them, or their Surveyor, or Clerk, shall attend at such Sessions; and the Justices in Sessions, upon due Proof of such Notice being given, and of the entering into such Recognizance, shall, on hearing the Evidence, finally determine whether the said Roads or Highways, so appealed against, shall be made, and shall

To prove the Allegations -of the said Petition, Mr.

David RuJJell being examined, said, That the Parish of Leeds is very extensive, and the Inhabitants thereof are become so numerous, that the Vicarage Church is much too small to contain them: That the Petitioner hath lately purchased a Building, finished and completed in a proper, decent, and very commodious Manner, fit for performing Divine Service therein; and that the Petitioner is desirous that the said Building may be consecrated, and set apart for such Service, and established as a Place of Divine Worship, according to the Usage of the Church of England, for ever — And the Witness further said, That the Petitioner hath obtained the Consent of the Vicar of the said Parish, and of the Trustees in whom the Patronage of the said Vicarage is veiled, and also of his Grace the Archbishop of Fork, the Ordinary thereof.

Sir Robert Buxton, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report which was made from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Common Brewers of the City of London, and the Parts adjacent, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed hirn to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, passed in the 33d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for "altering the Provisions of an Act, passed in the 22d -

" Year of the Reign of 11 is present Majesty, for repealing " the Duties payable for Beer and Ale above Six Shillings " the Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise, and not "exceeding Eleven Shillings the Barrel, exclusive of " such Duties, and for other Purposes therein mentioned;

" so far as respects the Quality of Table Beer brewed by " Common Brewers," as is expressed to be expedient in order to answer the Purpose of the said first-mentioned Act, has been proved, from the great Advance in Price on the Articles of Malt and Hops, as well as on the other constitiient Parts of the Capital of a Common Brewer, to be inadequate to the intended Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,.

That it is expedient, in order to answer the Purpose of the said Act, passed in the 22d Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, that the Common Brewer should be permitted to brew for Sale, Table Beer at a higher Price than Thirteen Shillings per Barrel, without the same being liable to any greater Duty than by the said Act of the 33d Year of His present Majesty, is payable for Table Beer brewed for Sale at Thirteen Shillings per Barrel, exclusive of the Duties of Excise.

A Petition of the Proprietors of the Coal Exchange, and of the Factors and Wholesale Buyers of Coals in the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; thu>|e4pmft Taking Notice of the Bill for repealing the several Acts speftingCoalt. now Force for preventing the Combination of Coal Owners, Lightermen, and Mailers of Ships, to advance the Price of Coals, and for preventing the Frauds and Abuses committed in the Admeasurement of Coals within the City of London and the Liberties thereof, and between Tower Dock and , in the County of Middlesex, and within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining thereto, and the several Parishes of Giles in the Fields, Saint Mary le Bone, and such Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew, Ho I born, as lies in the said County of Middlesex, and within the several Parishes lying between Putney and Rot her hit in the County of Surrey, and for making more effectual Provision for those Purposes; and for preventing the Impositions practised on Coalhcavers, on the River by Coal Under-

takers; and Setting forth. That the said Bill contains Clauses, which, if allowed to remain Part of the said Bill, will prove greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, and to the Trade in which they are engaged; and that the Mode of felling Cargoes of Coals in the Port of London, full Thirty Years ago, was by the Factors and Buyers assembling in the open Part or Area of Room Land, adjoining to the Fish Market of Billingsgate, each Day in the Week, and, when the Parties wishing to treat for a Cargo were met, for them to retire to some adjacent Tavern to conclude the Bargain, by which Mode of transacting Business great Inconvenience, and much Delay and Loss ot Time, -was felt by all Parties, when it was at length determined to erect the present Building called The Coal Exchange, by the Subscription of Sixty-tour Shares; and that it was proposed to charge each Ship, as Market Dues, for ever}' 50 Chaldron Cocket with is. which the Owners of the Cargoes voluntarily and cheerfully agreed to pay, each Party finding great Convenience by the Accommodation and Facility of

T Cl UlXtlCUl

Services in Ireland, deferred.

Petition of the Proprietors of the Coal Ex-

Irish Spirits Duty Bill, deferred.

transacting their Business; and that the Whole of the lower Part of the said Building was for many Years open for the assembling of all Descriptions of Persons, and the Sale of Cargoes were then made in each Factor's private Office, it being found impossible to conduct their Trade in the open Part of the said Building or Coal Market; and that at length, finding many Objections to the Bargains or Sales of Cargoes being made in the private Offices, and having found by Experience the Impossibility of concluding their Business in a Crowd of all Descriptions of Persons, Coalheavers, and others, it was by the Proprietors, at the Requell of the Trade, determined to inclose One Half of the lower Part of the said Building for an open Marker, where each Buyer might make his Offers, from which he was in some Degree precluded by the then Mode of the Sales being made in the private Offices; and the Number of the Trade having of late Y'ears very much increased, the Proprietors of the said Building have, at a very considerable Expence, just completed the Enlargement of the said Room or open Market for Coals, as they believe, to ihe Satisfaction of the whole Trade, with the Exception of very few Persons; and that every Person, of whatever Trade or Business, may enter the said Room, and transact what may be necessary to him for the Subscription of 6 each Market Day, or is. 6 d. Week, and for which he is accommodated with Fire, Pens, Ink, and Paper; and that the Petitioners conceive such Regulation cannot operate as a Bar to any Persons who have Business to transact in the said Market, and is only meant to keep out dirty or disorderly People; and that the Payment of the said Subscriptions, and Market Dues from the Ships, have never paid to the Proprietors Five Pounds per Cent, for their Capital lb expended in the Execution of the said Building or Coal Exchange, to the present Hour; and that the present Days of Business are Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, the same as the Corn Exchange^ and that those Days, from long Experience, have been found quite sufficient to expedite every Department of the said Trade, and which the Petitioners hope the House will find to be moll convenient, when it shall be proved to them, that the Business of Sales of each Day is generally done in one Hour, and that ioo, or even 200 Sail of Ships, if needful, can be fold in that Time; and that, if the present Days and Hours of Bu-finess were altered or increased, it would be attended with very serious Inconvenience to the Trade at large, and no possible Benefit to the Public would result from such Alteration: And therefore praying. That they may be heard against the Clauses of the said Bill, which are calculated to affect their Interests, by themselves, or their Counsel, to shew that such Clauses should not be permitted to Hand as Part of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

An Act for the better Collection of Rates made for the Relief of the Poor:

An Act for continuing, for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the Hand and Post in Upton Field, in the Parish of Burford, in the County of Oxford, to a Place in the Parish of Preston, in the County of Gloucester, called Dancy's Fancy:

Mr. Whitbread, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Expediency of exempting Curates, under certain Circumstances, from the Duty impoled by an Act, made in the 38th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for repealing the Duties upon Male Servants, Carriages, Horles, Mules,

" and Dogs; and for granting to His Majesty other " Duties in lieu thereof," upon Persons keeping One Horse, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that all Persons in Holy Orders, not assessed to the Duty on Income, should be permitted to keep One Horse only, for the Purpose of Riding, without being subject to the Duty granted by an Act, made in the 38th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, under certain Restrictions and Limitations.

The laid Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Licensed Victuallers, Alehouse-keepers, and Innkeepers, of the several Parishes of Saint Paul, S ha dwell, and Saint v in the County of

Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for repealing the several Acts now in Force for preventing the Combination of Coal Owners, Lightermen, and Matters of Ships, to advance the Price of Coals, and for preventing the Frauds and Abuses committed in the Admeasurement of Coals within the City of London, and the Liberties thereof, and between Tower Dock and Limehouse Hole, in the County of Middlesex, and within the City and Liberty of Wefuninftert and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining thereto, and the several Parishes of Saint Giles in the Fields, Saint Mary leBone, and such Part of the Purish of

Saint Andrew, Ho/horn, as lies in the said County of

Middlesex, and within the several Parishes lying between Putney and Rot her/,tithe, in the County of Surrey, and for making more effectual Provision for those Purposes; and for preventing the Impositions practised on Coalheavers, on the River Thames, by Coal Undertakers; and Setting forth. That the Coalheavers employed on the River Thames amount to upwards of One Thousand Men, and the Petitioners, from being allowed to act as Coal Undertakers, or Providers of Coalheavers, have had many and repeated Opportunities of affording Relief and Comfort to the Coalheavers, who worked from the Petitioners Houses, and particularly in relieving their Families in the Winter Time, and in the Time of their being out of Employ; and the Petitioners have given univerlal Satisfaction also to their Employers; and that, by giving to any particular Set of Men a Power exclusively of acting as Coal Undertakers, or limiting their Number to a few Individuals, the Petitioners conceive will not only be the Means of the Ruin of the Petitioners, and most of the Licensed Victuallers and Alehousekeepers contiguous to the Water Side, but will create a Monopoly in the providing Coallreavers to work the Ships out, and eventually tend to afford an Opportunity of practising Inipositions on the Coalheavers, and thereby an Injury to the Public at large: And therefore praying, That the House will take their same into Consideration; and allow the Petitioners to be heard, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

That by the Operation of the said Bill, if passed into a Law, the House and Shop in which the Petitioner now lives and carries on his Bu-finess, together with Five other Buildings situate in Saint Martin's Lane, will be wrested from him, without the Probability of his finding a Place in the Neighbourhood adapted to his Business, which mud suffer extremely by being transferred to any other Part of the Town; and that the annual Rent of the Five Buildings above-mentioned, though ancient and decayed, was £. 34. 10 s. till about Seven or Eight Years ago, since which Period their Produce has been very small, the Apprehensions of a Bill similar to the present preventing the Petitioner from felling, re-building, or converting them to any substantial Advantage; and that, so long ago as the Year 1796, the Petitioner made a Proposal to the Coir.missioners of Lamps and Scavengers in Birmingham of felling Three of the said Buildings or Tenements, at a moderate Price, for the Convenience of the Town, but then wished, and (till wilhes, to reserve Two of them for his own Accommodation, which are not, nor ever were, a Nuisance, as they leave the Street from Twenty-eight Feet and an Half to Thirty-one Feet wide, a Space not exceeded by other Parts which are to remain unmolested; and that the Petitioner, intending to remove his Business to this his Hereditary Freehold, being informed it was not included in the Bill, has taken Two of the said Buildings down at an Expence of nearly £.40, and, should the Bill pals, he is justly alarmed left he should not receive an adequate Compensation, as no Reference will be made to the Losses which he has sustained, or the Expence whiefv he has incurred; anefthat the Petitioner, willing to accommodate the Town, will resign for a fair Consideration Three of the said Buildings; and, though anxious to

That the Petitioners are great Sufferers by the Iniurreftion and Rebellion which happened in the IHand of Grenada in March 1795; and that the Petitioners have prepared a Petition to the House, praying for Relief on Account of the Lolfes they have iuftained; and that, from the particular Circumstances of their Cafe, and several recent Occurrences which have taken place, the Petitioners were not enabled to present their Petition within the Time limited by the Order of the House, for receiving Petitions; And therefore praying. That they may be permitted to present their said Petition, notwithstanding the Time is elapsed for presenting Petitions to the House,

Then a Petition of the Proprietors of Estates in the Wand of Grenada, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read j Setting forth. That the Petitioners are Proprietors of

Vol. 56.

Estates in the Wand of Grenada, which was ceded to the Crown of Great Britain by the Peace of 1763; and that the Petitioners were encouraged to adventure their Properties in the said Island, which, at the Time of its Cession, consisted almost Wholly of French Inhabitants, by the Protection held out by His Majesty's Proclamation for the Settlement of the ceded Wands in the West Indies; and that, notwithstanding the Cession of the Wand to Great Britain, the greatest Part of the French Inhabitants still retained their Ptoperties in the Wand, and, by taking the Oaths of Allegiance to His Majesty, availed themselves of the Protection of the British Government; and that in the Year 1779, the Wand was captured by a French Armament, under the Command of Count D'FJlaing,which Capture was in a great Measure imputable to the secret Correspondence carried on between the French Inhabitants and the Enemy, as appeared by Letters which had been intercepted; and that the Wand was restored to Great Britain by the Peace of 1783, when the British Inhabitants ' were so strongly impressed with an Opinion, founded on Experience, that the natural Attachment of the new Subjects was so rooted to the Government of France, that the Quiet of the Wand could only be maintained, in Time of Peace, by an effective Garrison, and that on the breaking out of any future War, the Wand would become the first Object of Attack; and that, under such Impression, one of the first Acts of the Legislature, after the Reftorarion, was to present a Memorial, on the Subject of an effective Garrison, to Lieutenant General Matthew, then Governor of the Iffand, in which they express, in the strongest Terms, the absolute Necessity of having such Militiary Protection as therein stated, and resolved, that even inconsiderable Expenditure of Public Money, for any Establishment which did not promise that Security, was injudicious and unwarranted; and that it appears, from the subsequent Correspondence between His Majesty's Government and the Legislature, that they continued to adhere to their first Resolutions, of not incurring any Expence towards the Erection of Fortifications, until they received positive Assurances of a competent Garrison for their Defence, and that upon such Assurances being given, they most chearfully complied with every Requisition made on the Part of Government for the Defence of the Wand, and expended, on that Account alone, considerably upwards of jf. 200,000 Sterling; and that, in consequence, the Garrison was augmented to 1,000 Men, the Force stated to be indispensibly necessary for the Defence of the Island, and which was continued until 1792, when Orders for withdrawing the 67th Regiment had been lent out, but, on a Memorial being presented by the Agent of the Wand, were immediately countermanded, which, the Petitioners humbly submit* was a full Confirmation of that Protection which the Legislature of Grenada had deemed absolutely necessary to the Safety of the Wand, and in perfect Conformity with the fair Import of the Correspondence and various Communications that had taken place on that Subject; and that, shortly after the breaking out of the present War, it was manifest that a great Part of the French Inhabitants, and nearly the Whole of the Free Negroes and, People of Colour, had most strongly imbibed republican and resolutionary Principles, and had actually kept up a traitorous Correspondence with the Common Enemy, and a coiisiderable Agitation was frequently apparent among them, which had often been communicated to the Lieutenant Governor, and particularly by a Message from the Council and Assembly of the Wand, in September 1794, and Application was in consequence made to the Commander in Chief for the Return of Part of their Garrison, which, up to February 1793, had consisted of the 45th and 67th Regiments, a Corps of Artillery, and the Carolina Black Troops, but, by various Draughts for other Services, were considerably reduced; but this Application did not procure them any Assistance; and

4 M that

ji. i8ot.

518 27* Apruis.

that for forne Months previous to March 1795, the Garrison had been so reduced, as at that Time not to muster 20b effective Men, which caused much Alarm in the Island, and was the Tubjedt of frequent Communications from the Council and Assembly to the Lieutenant Governor, expressive of their Fears for the Safety of the Colony, as exposed to Insurrection and Attack from the Enemy, as the very extensive Fortifications, without Troops to maintain them, served rather as an Incitement, than it operated as a Prevention to an Event so much dreaded; and that, in this Situation of the Island, on the 2d Day of March x 795, at Midnight, an-Insurred!ion broke out, which had been previously concerted, and had received the Countenance of the French Commissioners at Guad, who had mvefted the Leaders with Commissions from the French Nation, and had supplied them with Arms and Ammunition, and promised every Assistance they could afford them; and that the Plan of the Insurrection was kept so secret, and the Operations of the Insurgents were so conceited, for taking Place in different Parts of the Island at the same Period, that it was not until a considerable Time after it broke out that the Nature of it could be well ascertained; to attempt the Description of its Horror, or the Measure of its Ruin, Destruction, and Desolation, the Petitioners find themselves unable; in the short course of Five Weeks, hardly an Estate remained on which the Works and Buildings had not been burnt, the Cattle destroyed, the Crops despoiled, and the Negroes dif-perfect and driven to the Woods, upwards of Forty of the most respectable and wealthy Planters and Merchants among them; the Lieutenant Governor, and many Members of the Council and Assembly, were put to Death by the Insurgents with the most complicated Cruelty} the Numbers who afterwards fell in Battle, or died through excessive Fatigue, in defending the Fortifications of Saint George, by which Exertion, during the Space of Sixteen Months, they were alone enabled to maintain a Sovereignty in the Island, would be, in Truth to say, that more than Three-fourths of all the British Inhabitants of that Colony, upwards of 1,000 Persons, fell Victims to deliberate Murder, the Attacks of the Insurgents, or died through excessive Fatigue in performing Military Duty; and that these Calamities can with Truth be only imputed to the Weakness of the Garrison, from the Military Force being withdrawn from the Island for other Services, which, in the Event, proved as highly beneficial to this Kingdom as it was destructive to the Lives, Properties, and Prosperity of the Inhabitants of Grena, whose Losses, occasioned by the Insurrection, have been estimated, by a Committee of the Legislature appointed for that Purpose, at the Sum of £. 1,964,293. 153*/.; and that the Petitioners, therefore, with Confidence and Submission, here rest their Cafe, humbly hoping, that the Justice of their Claims, and the Humanity and Generality of a British Parliament, will afford them that Relief which has been granted to His Majesty's Subjects labouring under similar Calamities.

Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Bills for improving any City or Town, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Codd (Town Clerk of the said Town or Borough) being examined, said. That the Town of Kingston upon Hull is very large and populous, and a Place of consider-nble Trade; and that from the great Increase of Inhabitants, and of the Trade and Commerce thereof, the Market Place of the said Town has become too small, and the Streets called The Butchery, and Queen Street, near and leading to the said Market Place, are very narrow and incommodious. — And the Witness being further examined, said, That the Landing Places or Wharfs used for the Ferry Boats and Market Boats belonging to the said Town, are in a very inconvenient Situation, and, from the crowded state of that Part of the River Hull (the old Harbour) where such Boats usually lie, they are liable to Accidents, Damage, and Delay, and the Lives of Persons are thereby frequently endangered. — And the Witness added; That it would contribute much to the Convenience and Accommodation, as well of the Inhabitants of the said Town, as of all others resorting (hereto, if the Market Place were enlarged and improved, and divers Messuages, Tenements, Dwelling Houses, and 1

other Buildings, in the Streets called The Market Place,

Butchery, Queen Street, Blackfriar Gate, The Fore-Ropery,

The Back-Ropery, or Humber Street, in the same Town, were taken down, and a commodious Street made to extend from the Market Place aforesaid, to the River Humber, and a Dock or Bason made at the South End thereof, adjoining the said River, with a Landing Place or Wharf for the Accommodation of such Ferry Boats and Market Boats as aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging and improving the Market Place of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and for making a commodious Street trom the said Market Place to the River Humber, with a Dock and Wharf, or Landing Place, fqr the Ferry and Market Boats belonging and resorting to the said Town: And that Mr. Burdon, Mr. Wilberforce, and Mr. Henry Lascelles, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Burdon reported from the Committee, to whom Report re-the Report was re-committed, which was made from the Committee appointed to conllder of the Standing Orders eloiure Bill*, of the House, relative to Bills of Inclosure, lo tar as respects the letting out or the altering of public Roads,

and

and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had further proceeded in the Mat' ters to them referred, and had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read, and is as followed); v

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in all Bills for Inclosures there be inserted a Clause, by which the Commissioner or Commissioners shall be required to set'out the public Carriage Roads in such Directions as shall, upon the whole, appear to them most commodious for the Public, and to ascertain the same by Marks and Bounds, and to prepare a Map, in which such intended Roads shall be accurately laid down and described, and also such Carriage Roads, if any, as are intended, under the Powers which may be given by such Bill, to be flopped up, such Map, ligned by. the Commissioner, if only One, or the major Part of the said Commissioners, to be deposited with the Clerk of the said, Commissioner or Commissioners; and as soon as may be, after such Carriage Roads shall have been so set out, and such Map so deposited, to give Notice in some Newspaper to be named, circulating within that Part of the County where such intended Inclosure shall lie, which Notice shall also be affixed upon the Church Door of the Parish, of their having set out such Roads, and deposited such Map, and also of the general Lines of such intended Carriage Roads, and of the particular Carriage Roads, if any, so intended to be flopped, up, and to appoint, in the same Notice, a Meeting to be held by the Commissioner or Commissioners, at some convenient Place, in or near to the Parish or Township within which the Inclosure is to be made, and not sooner than Three Weeks from the Date of such Notice; at which Meeting any Perl'on who may be injured or aggrieved by the set ting out, or flopping up, of such Roads, may attend; and if any Person shall object to the setting out, or flopping tip, of the fame; that then the Commissioner or Commissioners shall hear and determine such Objection, and the Objections of any other such Person, to any Alteration that the said Commissioner or Commissioners may in consequence propose to make, and shall, according to their Judgment, upon the whole, order and direct how such Carriage Roads shall be set out, or flopped up, and either confirm the said Map, by resigning the fame, or jnake such Alterations therein, as the same may require; with a Proviso, that, if no Alteration shall be made by the said Commissioner or Commissioners, any Person lo having objected, or if any Alterations shall have been made, then such Person, or any other Person, who may be injured or aggrieved thereby, may appeal to some General Quarter Sessions of the Peace for the County, Riding, or Division, within Four Calendar Months next after such Meeting of the Commissioner or Commissioners as aforesaid, giving Notice, in Writing, to such Commissioner or Commissioners, or his or their Clerk, of the Intention to appeal, and of the Particulars to which he objects, and specifying the Alteration which he proposes, within Ten Days after such Meeting, and entering into a Recognizance, with sufficient Sureties, before a Justice of the Peace for the said County, to try the said Appeal; and requiring the said Commissioner or Commissioners further to cause such Notice to be published in the Newspaper before-mentioned, and also affixed on the Church Door of the said Parish; and that the said Commissioner or Commissioners, or One of them, or his or their Surveyor, or Clerk, shall attend at such Sessions, and then and there produce the Map above-mentioned; and the Juiliccs at Sessions, upon due Proof of such Notice being given, and of the entering into such Recognizance, shall, on hearing the Evidence, finally determine whether the said Roads, so appealed again!!, shall continue as halt ordered by the said Commissioner or Commissioners, or as proposed to be altered in such Notice, but not othenvile, and award such Costs to either Party,

_ \Oh. t.0.

as to them shall seem expedient; and such Determination of the said Justices shall be final, and shall not be removed; or removeable, by or otherwise;

but, in same no such Notice shall be given, or such Rei cognizance shall not be entered into, or such Appeal shall not be proceeded in as aforesaid, then such setting out, or flopping up, of the said Carriage Roads; by the said Commissioner or Commissioners as aforesaid, shall be final and conclusive.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Monday Morning next.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Richard Holden, Esquire, being examined, said, That the said Town of Rotherham is a populous and trading Town, and a public Market is and hath for Time immemorial been held there Once in every Week, and a public Fair twice in every Year; but that the present Market Place is very insufficient for the Purposes of the Market; and the Paffixgc along the public Streets is greatly obstru<5ied, and rendered inconvenient for Travellers and Passengers, by the Number of Stalls placed therein on Market Days, and the public Streets and Pallages are not sufficiently cleansed and lighted, and are subject to various Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances. — And the Witness further said, That it would be attended with very great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and others frequenting the said Market, if the present Market Place was enlarged, and a Market House with Butchers Shops, and other Shops, Slaughter Houses, and other Buildings were erected, and the Streets and Avenues leading thereto, widened, and improved, and a new Street opened thereto; and the several public Streets and Passages were properly cleansed and lighted, and other Improvements made in the said Town.

Mr. Abbot reported from thfe Select Committee, appointed to consider of the most effectual Means of promulgating the Statutes of the United Kingdom throughout all Parts of Great Britain and , and to report

the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and to whom the Report which, upon the 5th Day of December 1796, was made from the Committee appointed to consider of the most effectual Means of promulgating the Statutes of the Realm, was referred; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had come to several Resolutions thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read, and are as fob loweth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient, for the more general and speedy Promulgation of the Laws of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, that His Majesty's Printer should be authorized and directed to print not less than 5,500 Copies of every Public General Statute, and 306 Copies of every Public, Local, and Personal Statute.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer Ibould be authorized and directed to print and deliver (or transmit by the Post, or otherwise) so soon as possible after each Bill has received the Royal Assent, the aforesaid Number of 5,500 Copies of each Public General Statute, according to a Certain Mode of Distribution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer should be authorized and directed to print, and deliver or transmit in like Manner, the aforesaid 306 Copies of each Public, Local, and Personal Statute, according to a certain Mode of Distribution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Chief Magistrate and Head Officer of any City, Borough, or Town Corporate, in England and Ireland, and of every Royal Burgh in Scotland, and every Sheriff, Clerk of the Peace, and Town Clerk, in the United Kingdom of Great Bri and Ireland, receiving any such Copies, should preserv them for the Public Uie, and transmit them to his Successor in Oilice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of effectuating the Promulgation of Private Statutes (if the Parties interested therein shall think proper) and all'o for making Compensation to the Clerk of the Parliaments, and Oriicers of the House of Lords (in lieu of their annual Average Emoluments arising from the Office Copies of l'uch Statutes) without bringing any new Charge upon the Public, the Parties interested in every such Statute should make good such Expence and Compensation; and that thereupon such printed Copies of every such Statute should be made judicially admissible in Evidence, by adding thereto a Clause declaring the same to be a Public Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That His Majesty's Printer should also be authorized and directed to class the General Statutes, and the Public, Local, and'Personal Statutes of each Session, in separate Volumes, and to number the Chapters of each Clal's separately; and also, to print one General Title to each Volume, together with a General Table of all the Acts passed in that Session.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That such a'Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The laid Report is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

N.B. A printed Copy is with the Original.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of so much of an Act, made in the Parliament of Ireland, in the 40th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting, for One Year, the several Duties therein mentioned, in lieu of all other Duties payable upon the " Articles therein specified during the said Term; and " for regulating the Trade between this Kingdom and M His Majesty's Colonies; and for other Purposes therein mentioned," as relates to the Duties on Hops imported into Ireland, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion, of this Committee, That it is expedient to permit, for a limited Time, the Importation of Hops, the Growth or Produce of Great Britain, or of any Foreign Hops, into Ireland, upon the Payment of a Duty not exceeding One Penny Farthing for every Pound Weight thereof.

The laid Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question. put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolution; And that Mr. Corry, Mr. and

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Trustees for repairing the Turnpike1 Road from Dover to in the County of Kent, and also of several of the Inhabitants of the Town and Port of Dover, and the Town of Folke-stone, in the said County, and of the Gentlemen Farmers, and others, of the adjoining Neighbourhood, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for enlarging the Term, and altering the Powers, of Two Acts, one made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and the other made in the 4th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for amending, widening, and repairing, the Roads leading from Dover to Barham Downs, and from Cowgate and Archcliff Fort, in Dover, through to the Town of Hythe, in the County or Kent; and Setting forth. That the present Tolls are now vety iri« adequate to the Support of the Road, and an additional Toll Gate is necessary, and that any additional Toll to be collected at the present Gate, unless the -feme were very considerable, and extended to all- Horses and Car-, riages passing the fame,- not excepting those employed in Husbandry and Agriculture, would be totally blade- quate for the Purposes required; and if any such heavy Toll were laid, it is much to be feared that, from its being so oppressive, it would deter many Persons-from passing on that Part of the said Road, l'o that the Receipts on the Road would be diminished instead of being increased by the additional TolL; and that, for securing a proper and adequate Revenue for defraying the several Charges and Expences, it is absolutely necessary that a Toll Gate should be erected between Sea Brook Bridge and Hythe, in the Parish of Cheriton, that being the only Place where the Tolls can be rendered productive, and the Evasion of the Payment thereof be prevented;

by which means the Trustees hope to be enabled to pay off the Arrears of Interest so due, and to grow due, on the Security of the Tolls, and also to discharge their present Debts, and to enable them to widen the Road, and to make the necessary Repairs, and to fulfil their Duty to the Public: And therefore praying the House to take the Matter into Considerationf and to allow the Clause to stand in the said Bill for enabling the Trustees to ered a Toll Gate at the said Place called Sea Brook-, and that the Petitioners may be permitted-to be heard, by themselves, Agents, of Counsel, at the Committee, on the said Bill, in Favour thereof, or may have such other Relief in - the- Premises -as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Landholders, Hop Planters, and others, interested in the Cultivation of Hops, in the Counties of Kent and Sussex, was presented to the House, -and read; Setting forth. That Hops, from the Extent of their Cultivation in the Counties of Kent and Sussex, may be considered as forming the staple Commodity of those Counties; and that, independent of the Advantage derived to the Revenue, Hops have been admitted to be the raoft salutary Ingredient in the Bittering and Preservation of that useful Beverage, Beer; and that the System hitherto adopted of felling Hops in the private Houses of Factors, has tended to the Encouragement of Monopoly, and consequently to the great Injury and Inconvenience of the Public alt large, and the want of a public Market in or near the Metropolis, has long been universally acknowledged; and that the Establishment of such Market would, at the same Time that it accelerated the Sale of this Product, the moll expensive in its Cultivation of any other Species of Agriculture, essentially promote the Advantage of the Public, by affording a fair and general Competition; and that the necelfery Communications between the respective Counties, from their Extent, and the Numbers of Persons in-ierested, has unavoidably occasioned the Delay of an earlier Application to the House; and that it is eftential immediate Power should be given for the Establishment of such Market: And therefore praying. That they may have Leave to present a Petition for the Purpose of enabling them to bring in a Bill to establish an open 5

and public Market for the Sale of Hops, in the Borough

of Southwark, or in some other Situation adjacent thereto, as may be considered raoft eligible, in such Manner, and subject to such Rules and Regulations, as to this Honourable House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Chv cumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired.

Then a Petition of the Landholders, Hop Planters, and others, interested in the Cultivation of Hops; in the Counties of Kent and Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; containing the same Allegations as the last preceding Petition: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to establish an.open and public Market for the Sale of Hops, in the Borough of wark, or in some other Situation adjacent thereto, as may be considered most eligible, in such Manner, and subject to such Rules and Regulations, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the

Table.

Mr. John Fane reported from the Committee, to Whom the Petition of his Grace George Duke of Marlborough, and the humble Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Owners and Proprietors of Lands and Estates within the ToWnship of Beckley, and the Hamlets of Horton and Studley, in the Parish of Beckley, the Parish of Noke, the Parish of Oddington, the Township of Charlton, and the Hamlets of Fencott and Moorcott, in the Parish of Charlton, in the Counties of Oxford and Bucks, on Behalf of themselves, and other the Proprietors and Owners of Lands and Estates within the Parishes, Town-ships, and Hamlets aforesaid, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Drainage Bills, had been complied with, with respect to the affixing the Notices upon the Church Doors in all the said Parishes, on Sunday the 3d of last; but it appeared

to the Committee, that, on the following Sunday, the 10th of Attguft,the Person employed to affix the like

Notices was prevented from so doing at Beckley, Oddington, and Charlton, by a Mob at each Place, but that he read the Notices to the Persons assembled, and afterwards threw them amongst them into the Church Yards of thoie Parishes; and that the Notice was duly affixed, on that Day, upon the Church Door at Noke-, and that, on Sunday the 17th of the Person em-

ployed to put up the Notices was prevented from so doing, in regular Manner, at Beckley, and that at all the other Parishes he was likewise prevented on Account of the Mob, but that he read the Notices to the Persons there assembled, and afterwards threw them amongst them into the Church Yards; and that the Committee had also examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Alexander Niven being examined, said. That there is within the said Parishes, or some or one of them, a certain Low Common or Waste, called Otmoor, containing about 4,000 Acres, and that the Petitioners, with others, the Owners and Proprietors of Lands and VoL. 56.

Estates within the Township of Beckley, and the Hamlets of Horton and Studley, within the Parish of Beckley, and within the other Parishes and Places, have a Right of Common upon the said Common or Waste; and that the same is overflowed with Water a considerable

Part of the Year, and during such Time is of little or no Use to the Proprietors, but that the same is capable of being drained, and by that Means much improved in Value. — And the Witness further said, That by Reason of the great Extent of the said Moor, and the Intermixture of the Cattle of the Inhabitants of the different Parishes and Places, much Inconvenience arises. — And the Witness added, That the Petitioners are desirous* that the said Common should be drained and divided into so many Parts as there are distinct Parishes, Townships, or Hamlets, and amongst the several Persons having a Right of Common upon the fame, which would be to the great Advantage of all Parties interested therein, and to the Benefit of the Public.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for draining and improving the Common, or Waste, called Otmoor, within the Township of Beckley, and the Hamlets of Horton and Studley, in the Parish of Beckley, in the Parishes of Noke and Oddington, the Township of Charlton, and the Hamlets of Fencott and Moorcott, in the Parish of Charlton, in the Counties of Oxford and Bucks, or some or one of them, and for dividing, and setting out, specific Parts thereof, for the several Pa-riflies, Townships, and Hamlets respectively, and amongst the several Persons having a Right of Common thereon, or interested therein: And that Mr. John Fane and Lord Francis Almaric Spencer do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the 33d Year of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Communication from the Junction of the River Fofs with the River Ouse, at or near the City of Fork, to Stillington in the

Parish of Stillington, in the North Riding of the County of York, and for draining and improving certain Low Lands, lying on each Side of the said River Fofs, was read; whereby it appeared, that certain Persons therein named and described, were incorporated by the Name of " The Fofs Navigation ," with Power to make

and maintain the said Navigation, and Provision was also made by the said Act, for draining and improving the said Low Lands: That by the said Act, the said Company were empowered to raise and contribute, amongst themselves, such Sum and Sums of Money as they should find sufficient for making and completing the said Navigation; and also the several Works of Drainage therein mentioned, not exceeding in the whole, the Sum of £.25,400, except that, if the said Sum should be found insufficient for the Purposes aforesaid, then the said Company might raise amongst themselves, or by the Admission of new Subscribers, any further Sum or Sums of Money, not exceeding the Sum of £. 10,000; or that the said Company might, if they thought proper, borrow any Part of the said Sum of £. 10,000 on the Credit of the said Undertaking. — Then,

Mr. Thomas Plummer being examined, said. That the said Company have proceeded in making and completing certain Parts of the said Navigation and Drainage by the said Act authorized to be made, and have raised and expended not only the whole of the said Sum of £.25,400, but a further Sum of Money, which they have borrowed on Mortgage of the said Undertaking, as Part of the said Sum of £.10,000; and they have also incurred sundry Debts, as well for Lands marked, set out, or taken and used, for the said Navigation, and the Works appertaining thereto, as for divers Materials, Utensils, and Implements, used in the Prosecution of the said Undertaking, and are now greatly in Arrear to the several Mortgagees, for the Interest on their respective Securities: That the Company have used their utmost Endeavours to borrow on Mortgage, as aforesaid, the Residue of the said Sum of £. 10,000, but have not been able to procure the Loan thereof, and the Creditors of the said Company are not only very pressing for the Principal and Interest due to them, but several of them have given Notice of their Intention of enforcing Payment of their Demands by Law. — And the Witness being further examined, said. That the said Company, unless they are enabled to raise and enforce the Payment amongst themselves, of a larger Sum of Money than they are at present empowered to do, will be totally unable to liquidate and discharge the said Debts by them so contracted and incurred, or to complete the said Navigation and other Works, or maintain and uphold so much thereof as is now finifljed: Vol. 56.

That the said Act hath in several respects been found defective, and the Execution of feme of the Powers and - Provisions thereof, in the Mode prescribed, inconvenient with respect to the Navigation thereby authorized and directed to be made, completed, and maintained; and it is requiflte that the same should be altered and amended.

Sir William El ford reported from the Committee, to Koop't Patent whom the Petition of Matthias K, of James Street, in the Parish of Saint Margaret, Westminster, in the F County of Middlesex, Gentleman, was referred; That the

Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioner said, That he had prepared a particular Specification of his Invention for making Paper from Straw,

Hay, Thistles, Walles, and Refuse of Hemp and Flax, and different kinds of Wood and Bark, fit for Printing, and other useful Purposes, to be inrolled in pursuance of the Proviso contained in the Letters Patent mentioned in the said Petition; but is informed, that if the same be inrolled in the Court of Chancery, there is no Means of preventing Copies being obtained by Foreigners and others, who will thereby have the Advantage over His Majesty's Subjects, by making Use of the same in Foreign Countries, as many Instances are known to the Petitioner, of Inventions, for which Letters Patent have been obtained in this Country, having been carried on Abroad, in consequence of Copies of Specifications being obtained here of such Inventions, and particularly Sir Richard Arkwright's Invention of Engifies for Carding and Spinning of Cotton, having been ella-blished in Prussia and several Parts of Germany. — And the Petitioner produced to Your Committee, Two Volumes of a Publication, called " The Repertory of Arts:

" and Manufactures," published in Numbers Monthly, since the Year 1794; which contains Copies of Specifications of Patents obtained for Inventions and Machinery in this Kingdom, and Plates of such Machinery; and which Work is constantly carried to the Continent, and there tranllated into the French, German, and other Languages; whereby Foreigners are enabled tp avail themselves of the Inventions of Men of Genius and Science in this Kingdom, to the great Detriment and Injury of the Public, the Revenue, and the Inventors;

and that in the Monthly Numbers of such Work for Marsh last, a Copy of the Specification of the Invention of the Petitioner, for extracting Writing and Printing Ink from written and printed Paper, converting the same into Pulp, and re-manufact using the same into Paper again, and for which Invention His Majesty was pleased to grant the Petitioner Letters Patent, is inserted. — -The Petitioner further Hated to Your Committee, That he had been informed, that in Letters Patent granted for Ireland, there was no restrictive Proviso contained therein, as to the Number of Persons to be concerned therein, as there is in those granted for England and for Scotland. — Then,

duced a Copy of another Warrant signed by His Majesty, the Original of which he stated to have been sent to Ireland,authorizing and requiring His Majesty's Lord Lieutenant there to cause good and sufficient Letters Patent to be palfed under the Great Seal of Ireland, giving unto the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, His Special Licence, during the Term of Fourteen Years from the Date thereof, to vend his said Invention within Ireland, and which Warrant is stated to Your Committee to bear Date on the 22d Day of January last; and also produced a Deed of Agreement executed between the Right honourable Earl Grosvenor, the Petitioner and others, for the De-

mile of certain Lands at Millbank, belonging to his Lordship, for a certain Term therein mentioned, to the Petitioner and others, for the Purpose of carrying on the Manufacture mentioned in the Petition, and in which the Petitioner and others covenant to pay his Lordship a clear Annual Rent of'£.1,000.; and also, to lay out and expend on the Premises, in Erections for carrying on the said Manufacture, previous to requiring the said Demise to be made to them, the Sum of £. z 5,000. — Then,

John Hunter, Esquire, being examined, said, That to carry on the Manufacture mentioned in the Petition, would require a Sum of Money far beyond the Means or Power of the Petitioner to bring forward; and that he knew several Gentlemen who were ready to hazard and subscribe nearly £.100,000, for the Purpose of establishing and carrying on the said Manufacture, on being permitted to participate in and enjoy the Liberties and Privileges granted to the Petitioner by the said Letters Patent; but that no Five Persons would come forward to hazard such a Sum. — Then,

Mr. John Rennie, an Engineer, being examined, said. That the Works necessary, and already ordered to be built, for the Purpose of carrying on the said Manufacture, together with the Steam Engine, Utensils, and Machinery, will cost about £.50,000. — Then,

Mr. Benjamin Cooper, a Surveyor, being examined, said. That he had prepared Plans for the different Buildings necessary for carrying on the said Manufacture, the Expence of which Buildings will cost about £. 50,000. — Then,

Mr. Elias Carpenter, Paper Maker, being examined, laid, That not less than Five Hundred Persons would be employed, in the first Instance, in the said Manufacture, and on the Scale on which it was purposed to establish it, he believed not less than Eight hundred or One thousand Persons.would be necessary; that Three-fourths of the Rags consumed in this Coun-

try is supplied from Abroad; which, by this Manufacture, would in a great measure be rendered unnecessary; and that he has not the least Doubt, but that this Manufacture, if established, will considerably reduce the Price of Paper, as it can be carried to any Extent: That the Scarcity of Rags has been l'o great as to prevent the Paper Makers from executing their Orders at any Price, and the Buyer would have been a Loser if he had taken the Paper at even Half the advanced Price the Paper Maker could have afforded to fell it at. — He produced to Your Committee several Samples of Paper which were made by him, under the Direction of the Petitioner, and which were made solely from Straw and Wood, without the Mixture of any other Article.

Mr. Thomas Burton, Printer to the Tax Office, being then examined, said. That in July 1799, he had not less than Three Prefles standing Hill for the want of Paper. — Then,

Mr. Charles Cooke, a Book feller in Pater Nojler Row, being examined, said, That such is the high PriGe of the Raw Material with which Paper is now made, that he could not print the detached Numbers to complete different Sets of Works he bad advertised to publish, without being at a greater Expence in printing the same than what he fold them for.

Then a Member present informed Your Committee, That the House, in which he is a Partner, pays to Foreigners, Money on Letters of Credit given on them, many of which are to Persons sent to inspect the Manufactories and Inventions established in this Country:-That such Persons frequently inquire where such are established, and alk for Letters of Recommendation from them, to different Residents who live in those Places where they are set up; and he believes it to be a Matter of great Notoriety that such Practices exist, and, he believes, much to the Prejudice of the Manufactures of this Country. — Then,

Mr. James Chalmers, being examined, said, That after the Specifications of Inventions are inrolled in the Chancellary of Scotland, Extracts, or Copies thereof, may be obtained by any Person who applies for the lame, on paying the usual Fees, which are of small Amount.

Then Mr. James Poole, being examined, said. That he had been Clerk of the Patent Office in England upwards of Seventeen Years last part, and that when Specifications are enrolled in the Offices directed by Letters Patent, Foreigners, or any other Persons, may obtain Copies thereof, by paying certain accustomed Fees, which are small.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon ThursdayMorning next.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to continue for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and alter and enlarge the Powers, of Two Acts, passed in the Thirty-second Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road from the Cross at Broken Cross, in Macclesfield, in the County of Chester, to the Turnpike Road at Buxton, in the County of , and for making and keeping in Repair certain Branches of Road to communicate with the said Macclesfield Road; without any Amendment i And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making and maintaining a Road from the Town of New WindJ'or, in the County of Berks, into the London Road, at or near a Bridge called High Bridge near Longford, in the County o f BQiddlesexand for amending, widening, and keeping in Repair, the Road leading from and out of the said ILad at South ley, in the Parish of Datchet, to the Village of Datchet, in the County of Bucks-, without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open and Common Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Wastes, and other Commonable Linds and Grounds, within the Parish of Wrefilingworth, in the County of Bedford -, with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.
